posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha in December: snow, temperatures, crowds and what to pack, with notes from the mountain guides who lead it.
posts.body:
December is a great month for Kedarkantha if you want your first real snow trek and don't mind company. Most years, the first proper snowfall arrives during the month and turns the upper trail white. The catch is the crowd: the week between Christmas and New Year is the busiest of the whole season.

The best way to do December well is to go early or mid-month, on weekdays if you can. December departures, with seats left, are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Will there be snow on Kedarkantha in December?

Usually, yes, but how much and when varies from year to year.

- **Early December:** often patchy snow near the top, with a dry or frosty trail through the forest.
- **Mid to late December:** most years, at least one good snowfall has happened by now, and the trail from around Juda ka Talab upwards is under snow.
- **Some years:** snow comes late, in the last week of December or even January. It's not common, but it happens.

So December is a reasonable bet for snow, but it isn't a guarantee. Check our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) a week or two before you go, and look at photos from the previous week rather than last year's.

When it has snowed, December snow is usually fresh and soft. It's beautiful, but slower to walk through than the firmer snow of February.

## How cold is Kedarkantha in December, by day and at night?

December is properly cold, especially from the middle of the month.

- **Sankri:** days 8°C to 12°C, nights −2°C to 2°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 4°C to 9°C, nights −5°C to −8°C
- **Base camp:** days 2°C to 7°C, nights −8°C to −12°C

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

December has the shortest days of the year. It's dark by about 5:15 pm, so you spend a long evening at camp in the cold. Summit morning is very cold, often below −10°C before sunrise, colder with wind. Full details in [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)

## How crowded is the Kedarkantha trail in December?

December has two very different halves.

1 to about 20 December: busy on weekends, reasonable on weekdays. This is the sweet spot of the month.

About 21 December to 2 January: the peak of the season. School holidays, Christmas and New Year all fall together, and huge numbers of people head to Kedarkantha. Campsites fill up, the trail can feel like a queue near the summit, and the road to Sankri gets busy too.

Some people love the festive atmosphere of a New Year's Eve in the snow. Others find it the opposite of why they came to the mountains. Decide which you are before you book. Our thoughts on crowding are in [Is overcrowding ruining popular treks like Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-crowded), and our [weekly crowd report](/blog/kedarkantha-crowd) shows the current picture.

If you want to trek over the holidays but avoid the worst of it, look at other winter treks too: [Where can you trek over Christmas and New Year in India?](/blog/christmas-new-year-treks-uttarakhand-himachal)

## What should you pack for Kedarkantha in December?

December is full winter kit time.

- Down jacket rated to −10°C, or a −5°C jacket with a good fleece and thermal under it.
- **Two layers of gloves:** thin liners and warm waterproof outers. Wet gloves are the most common complaint in December.
- **Gaiters:** helpful if there's fresh snow. We provide them when conditions need them.
- **Microspikes:** often needed on summit day once snow has packed into ice. We carry them and your mountain guide hands them out.
- **Sunglasses with real UV protection:** fresh snow reflects a lot of light.
- **Spare socks:** at least one extra pair, kept dry in a plastic bag.
- **Insulated bottle:** water freezes at base camp overnight.

The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list)

## What is it like to spend Christmas and New Year on Kedarkantha?

Many people choose Kedarkantha for the holiday week, and it can be a memorable way to end the year: snow on the ground, cold clear nights and a summit at dawn. It also comes with trade-offs worth knowing before you book.

- **Busy campsites.** The last week of December is the busiest stretch of the season. Juda ka Talab and base camp can host many groups at once, and the summit trail can turn into a long line of headtorches.
- **Early bookings.** Holiday departures, buses and trains to Dehradun fill weeks in advance. So do guesthouses in Sankri.
- **Higher prices.** Many operators charge more for holiday-week departures, and taxis cost more too.
- **A festive mood, with limits.** Groups celebrate with cake and songs in the dining tent. Alcohol isn't allowed on our treks, and it's a bad idea at altitude anyway ([Is it safe to drink alcohol on a high-altitude trek?](/blog/alcohol-on-trek)).

If you want snow but not the crowds, the first three weeks of December are usually a better bet. Either way, carry your rubbish back down; the holiday weeks leave the most litter on the trail ([What does Leave No Trace mean on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/leave-no-trace)).

## Tips for a good Kedarkantha trek in December

1. **Book early if you want holiday dates.** Christmas and New Year departures fill weeks in advance, and so do buses and trains to Dehradun.
2. Prefer the first three weeks if you want snow without the crowds.
3. **Leave a buffer day on your return.** Fresh snow or traffic can slow the road from Sankri.
4. **Train before you go.** Fresh December snow makes the walking slower and harder than the same trail in November ([How do you train for a trek in four weeks?](/blog/4-week-trek-training-plan)).
5. **Expect long evenings.** Bring a book, cards or something to pass the time after dark.

## What is Kedarkantha summit day like in December?

December has the shortest days of the year, so summit day starts in full darkness and the sun rises late, around 7 am. You'll walk for two to three hours by headtorch, in temperatures often around −10°C before dawn.

Underfoot, it depends on the snow. Early in the month, the summit slope may be patchy, with frozen ground and icy spots in the shade. After the first big snowfall, the snow can be soft and fresh, which is beautiful but slower to walk through. Microspikes and gaiters are handed out when your mountain guide decides they're needed.

The descent is where most people slip. Take short steps, keep your weight over your feet and use your poles. More on the climb in [How high is Kedarkantha peak, and how hard is summit day?](/blog/kedarkantha-height)

## Is December or January better for Kedarkantha?

### Kedarkantha in December

- **Snow:** Usually arrives during the month
- **Cold:** Very cold
- **Crowds:** Very high at the end of the month
- **Snow texture:** Often fresh and soft

### Kedarkantha in January

- **Snow:** Usually well established
- **Cold:** Coldest month
- **Crowds:** High in the first week, then lower
- **Snow texture:** Settled, firmer underfoot

If snow is the priority and the holidays aren't, January and February are more reliable. See [Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in January?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-january) and the full month-by-month view in [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)

For everything else, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide). December dates and seats left are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in January?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek in January: Snow, Cold, Crowds
posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha in January: snow, temperatures, crowds and what to pack, with notes from the mountain guides who lead it.
posts.body:
January is Kedarkantha in full winter: the coldest nights, snow from the forest to the summit in most years, and a trail that feels far from everything. It's the month to choose if you want a true snow trek and you're ready to prepare for real cold. After the first week, when the New Year crowds leave, it also gets noticeably quieter. January dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Will there be snow on Kedarkantha in January?

In most years, yes, and plenty of it. By January several snowfalls have usually built up on the upper trail, and fresh storms keep adding to it through the month.

- **On the trail:** snow often starts somewhere in the forest between Sankri and Juda ka Talab and continues all the way to the top.
- **Juda ka Talab:** usually frozen solid by January ([Is Juda ka Talab frozen in winter?](/blog/juda-ka-talab)).
- **Base camp and summit:** deep snow, sometimes knee-deep after a fresh fall.

Dry winters do happen, and then even January can be thinner on snow than you'd hope. Our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) tells you what's really there before you travel.

Snow in January tends to be powdery after a fresh fall and firm in the early mornings. That firm morning snow is actually easier to walk on than the slushy afternoon snow of March.

## How cold is Kedarkantha in January, by day and at night?

January is the coldest month on Kedarkantha.

- **Sankri:** days 5°C to 10°C, nights −4°C to 0°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 2°C to 7°C, nights −6°C to −10°C
- **Base camp:** days 0°C to 5°C, nights −10°C to −15°C

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

On summit morning, starting before sunrise, temperatures of −12°C to −15°C are common, and wind can make it feel like −20°C. Inside your tent, frost forms on the walls overnight and water bottles freeze unless you keep them in your sleeping bag.

It sounds tough, and it is, for a few hours each day. In the sunshine, though, January days can be surprisingly pleasant for walking. Most of the hard cold is in the evening, the night and the hour before sunrise. More in [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)

## How crowded is the Kedarkantha trail in January?

- **1 to about 5 January:** still busy with the tail end of the New Year rush.
- **The rest of January:** busy on weekends, much calmer on weekdays.
- **26 January long weekend (Republic Day):** another busy spell when it falls next to a weekend.

Mid-January weekdays are some of the most peaceful snow days of the season. If you can take time off midweek, this is a very good window. Our [weekly crowd report](/blog/kedarkantha-crowd) shows the current numbers.

## What should you pack for Kedarkantha in January?

January needs your warmest kit. Don't cut corners here.

- Down jacket rated to −10°C or colder. If yours is lighter, add a thick fleece and a thermal under it.
- Thermal top and bottom, plus a spare dry set for sleeping.
- Two pairs of gloves: liners and insulated waterproof outers, plus a spare pair of liners.
- Balaclava or neck gaiter for summit morning wind.
- Waterproof trekking shoes with deep grip, broken in well before the trek.
- Gaiters and microspikes: we provide them when conditions need them, which in January is often.
- Insulated water bottle, or a bottle you can fill with hot water to warm your sleeping bag.
- Hand warmers: small, cheap and very welcome on summit morning (optional).

The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list), and night tips are in [How do you sleep warm in a tent in minus temperatures?](/blog/sleeping-warm-in-tent)

## How snow changes the Kedarkantha walk in January

Snow makes everything a little slower. Expect your walking days to take 30 minutes to an hour longer than the times on the itinerary, especially after a fresh snowfall. Your mountain guide may adjust the summit start time depending on conditions.

The descent on summit day is where people slip most often in January. Walk in the footsteps of the person ahead, keep your weight over your feet, and use poles. Our guide to [walking on snow without slipping](/blog/walking-on-snow) is worth reading before you go.

If heavy snow falls during your trek, the team may wait a day or change plans for safety. It's rare, but leave a buffer day in your travel plans just in case.

## How to stay warm on Kedarkantha in January

January is the coldest month on Kedarkantha, so staying warm is a skill worth practising from day one.

1. **Layer up and down through the day.** Remove a layer before you start sweating on the climb, and add one the moment you stop.
2. **Change into dry clothes as soon as you reach camp.** Damp socks and base layers are what make people cold.
3. **Protect your hands and feet first.** Wear liner gloves under waterproof outer gloves, and keep a dry pair of woollen socks only for sleeping.
4. **Eat and drink often.** Hot soup, tea and regular snacks keep your body making heat.
5. Take a hot-water bottle into your sleeping bag, and keep your phone and power bank inside it too, so the cold doesn't drain them.
6. **Cover your face on summit morning.** A balaclava or neck gaiter stops the wind from burning your cheeks.

More detail is in [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)

## Is Juda ka Talab frozen in January?

Usually, yes. In most years, the lake at Juda ka Talab is frozen over through January, with snow on the ice and on the forest around it. It's one of the most photographed sights on the trek. Enjoy it from the edge: the ice can be thinner than it looks, and walking on it isn't safe. The story behind the lake is in [Is Juda ka Talab on the Kedarkantha trek frozen in winter?](/blog/juda-ka-talab)

## Who should do Kedarkantha in January?

Good for:

- Trekkers who want the most wintry version of Kedarkantha
- People who prepare well and like a challenge
- Anyone who can travel midweek and wants quiet snow

Think twice if you:

- Really dislike cold, or have had trouble with cold hands and feet before
- Are trekking with young children
- Can't train beforehand; deep snow makes the trek harder

If cold is a worry, consider late February or March ([Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)).

## Is January or February better for Kedarkantha?

### Kedarkantha in January

- **Snow:** Deep, often fresh
- **Cold:** Coldest month
- **Crowds:** Busy first week, then lower
- **Days:** Short

### Kedarkantha in February

- **Snow:** Deep and settled
- **Cold:** Very cold, easing late in the month
- **Crowds:** Generally lower
- **Days:** A little longer

Both are excellent for snow. January is more raw and wintry; February is a touch kinder. Read [Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in February?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-february) to compare.

For the full trek overview, see [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide). January dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in February?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek in February: Snow, Cold, Crowds
posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha in February: snow, temperatures, crowds and what to pack, with notes from the mountain guides who lead it.
posts.body:
February is the month many experienced trekkers quietly pick for Kedarkantha. The snow is usually at its deepest and most settled, the holiday crowds are long gone, and by the last week the days begin to soften. If you want a proper snow trek without sharing every campsite, February is hard to beat. February departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Will there be snow on Kedarkantha in February?

In a normal winter, yes, and lots of it. By February the trail has had a whole season of snowfall, and the layers have packed down into a firm base.

- **From Sankri:** the lower forest may be clear or patchy, depending on the year.
- **Around Juda ka Talab:** usually under snow, with the lake frozen ([Is Juda ka Talab frozen in winter?](/blog/juda-ka-talab)).
- **Base camp and summit:** deep snow, often the deepest of the season.

Fresh storms still arrive in February, sometimes dropping a lot of snow in a day or two. After a storm, the trail can take a little while to be broken in again, and walking is slower. Our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) shows what fell last week and how the trail looks.

The big advantage of February snow is its texture. In the early morning it's firm and crunchy, which makes summit day easier underfoot than the soft, fresh snow of December.

## How cold is Kedarkantha in February, by day and at night?

Still very cold, especially in the first half of the month, but a touch easier than January.

- **Sankri:** days 7°C to 12°C, nights −3°C to 1°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 3°C to 8°C, nights −5°C to −9°C
- **Base camp:** days 1°C to 6°C, nights −8°C to −13°C

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

Days are already noticeably longer than in December, so you have more daylight at camp and a little less time sitting in the cold after dark. Summit morning remains bitter: plan for −10°C or below before sunrise, and colder if there's wind. See [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature) for how to dress.

## How crowded is the Kedarkantha trail in February?

February is one of the calmest snow months on Kedarkantha.

- **Weekdays:** often quiet, sometimes very quiet.
- **Weekends:** steady but rarely packed.
- **Exception:** any long weekend, and the last week of February in years when college holidays begin early.

This is the main reason February works so well. The trail and the snow are at their best while most people are back at work or in exams. You'll have space at camp, quiet on the summit and a pace that suits your group. For the bigger picture, see [Is overcrowding ruining popular treks like Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-crowded)

## What should you pack for Kedarkantha in February?

Pack full winter kit, as you would for January.

- Down jacket rated to −10°C, or a lighter one with a good fleece and thermal under it
- Two layers of gloves and a spare pair of liners
- Waterproof trekking shoes with deep grip
- Gaiters, which keep deep snow out of your shoes (we provide them when needed)
- Microspikes for icy morning snow on summit day (we carry them and hand them out)
- Good sunglasses and SPF 50: February sun on deep snow is strong, and longer days mean more glare
- A light layer for the afternoon: by late February, the walk back from the summit can feel warm in the sun

The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list)

## Early or late February: which is better for Kedarkantha?

The month changes as it goes.

### Kedarkantha in the first half of February

- **Snow:** Deep, sometimes fresh
- **Nights:** Very cold
- **Days:** Short
- **Crowds:** Low

### Kedarkantha in the second half of February

- **Snow:** Deep, more settled
- **Nights:** Cold, slowly easing
- **Days:** Longer, warmer in the sun
- **Crowds:** Low, except long weekends

If you feel the cold badly, aim for the second half. If you want the most wintry version, go early. Either way, check the forecast before you leave and pack for snow.

## What the Kedarkantha trail looks like in February

February is Kedarkantha at its most complete as a snow trek. In a normal year, snow covers the trail from the forest above Sankri all the way to the summit. The pines carry snow on their branches, Juda ka Talab is usually frozen and white, and base camp sits in a wide, open snowfield with the summit cone above it.

Between storms, the sky is often a deep, clear blue, and the low winter sun throws long shadows across the snow in the late afternoon. It's a wonderful month for photographs. Keep your sunglasses on whenever you're on snow, and keep your phone warm in an inside pocket so the battery lasts.

## What to expect on Kedarkantha summit day in February

February summit days usually start a little later than December's, because sunrise comes earlier, but the plan is the same: leave base camp in the dark, climb steadily, reach the top around sunrise. The firm morning snow often makes the climb feel easier than people expect. The descent is the part to take carefully, because the sun softens the snow by late morning and it can turn slippery.

Our [guide to walking on snow](/blog/walking-on-snow) has a few simple techniques that help a lot.

## Tips for trekking Kedarkantha in February

1. **Pack for full winter.** Nights at base camp can still drop below −10°C, especially early in the month.
2. **Wear gaiters and waterproof shoes.** Deep snow gets into ordinary shoes quickly.
3. Use microspikes on the summit slope and the descent. Your team should provide them in winter.
4. Pick a weekday start for the quietest trail, and avoid any long weekend if you can.
5. **Leave a buffer day at the end.** A February snowstorm can delay the summit or slow the road.
6. **Look after your skin and eyes.** Sun on snow burns quickly, even when the air is freezing.

## Is February the best month for Kedarkantha?

For most people, it's the best balance of snow, quiet and manageable cold. It's not the right choice if you can only cope with mild weather, in which case look at [March](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-march) or [April](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-april-and-may). Compare it with [January](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-january), or see every month side by side in [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)

The full overview of the trek is in [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide), and February dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in March?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek in March: Snow, Cold, Crowds
posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha in March: snow, temperatures, crowds and what to pack, with notes from the mountain guides who lead it.
posts.body:
March is a good month for Kedarkantha if you want snow near the top but kinder weather overall. The lower trail starts to melt out, the days are warmer and longer, and the nights, while still cold at base camp, no longer feel brutal. It's a strong choice for anyone who finds December and January too harsh. March dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Will there be snow on Kedarkantha in March?

Usually on the upper half of the trek, less so below.

- **Sankri to the lower forest:** often clear of snow by March, or with old patches in the shade.
- **Around Juda ka Talab:** patchy to full snow, depending on how heavy the winter was. The lake may still be frozen early in the month and thawing later.
- **Base camp and summit:** snow in most years, sometimes plenty of it.

March can also bring fresh snowfall. A late storm can cover the whole trail again for a few days, so don't be surprised if your photos look like January.

The main thing that changes is the snow's texture through the day. In the early morning it's frozen hard. By late morning the sun softens it, and by afternoon it can be wet and slushy. This is why March summit days still start early: you want to climb and descend while the snow is firm.

Check our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) before you go. March varies more from year to year than any other month.

## How cold is Kedarkantha in March, by day and at night?

Milder than mid-winter, but still cold at night up high.

- **Sankri:** days 12°C to 18°C, nights 2°C to 5°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 7°C to 12°C, nights −2°C to −5°C
- **Base camp:** days 4°C to 10°C, nights −4°C to −8°C

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

Walking in the day is comfortable, often in a T-shirt and light fleece. Evenings at base camp still need your down jacket, and summit morning is cold before sunrise. The difference from January is that the cold doesn't last as long, and you warm up quickly once the sun is out.

## How crowded is the Kedarkantha trail in March?

March is generally quiet on Kedarkantha.

- **Early March:** low numbers, with some weekend groups.
- **Holi weekend:** can be busy if it creates a long weekend.
- **Late March:** low, as many people think the snow season is over.

That last point works in your favour. Plenty of trekkers assume snow is gone by March, so the trail stays calm even when the upper slopes are still white.

## What should you pack for Kedarkantha in March?

March packing sits between winter and spring.

- **Down jacket:** still needed for evenings and summit morning. A −5°C jacket is usually enough.
- **Light layers:** you'll walk warmer in the day, so quick-dry T-shirts and a light fleece matter more.
- **Waterproof shoes:** melting snow means wet, muddy trail in places. Waterproof shoes and gaiters keep your feet dry.
- **Extra socks:** feet get wet in slush. Carry at least two spare pairs.
- **Microspikes:** we carry them for icy early-morning sections.
- **Sun protection:** strong sun on snow. SPF 50, lip balm and good sunglasses are essential.
- **A rain layer:** March weather can turn, and a passing shower or snow flurry is common in the afternoon.

The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list)

## What the Kedarkantha trail looks like in March

March is the month of change on Kedarkantha. Early in the month it can still look like deep winter above Juda ka Talab, with snow on the forest floor and a white base camp. As the weeks pass, the snowline climbs. The lower forest turns to wet earth and patches of old snow, Juda ka Talab starts to thaw at the edges, and the first rhododendrons may flower in the lower forest late in the month, depending on the year.

Above the treeline, the slopes usually stay white through March, so you still get a snowy summit and base camp. Days are noticeably longer and warmer than in February, and on a clear afternoon you can sit outside your tent in the sun.

## Things to know about Kedarkantha in March

1. **Start early every day.** Firm snow in the morning is much easier and safer than wet snow in the afternoon.
2. **Expect mud lower down.** The melt makes parts of the forest trail soft and slippery. Walk carefully and use poles.
3. **Weather changes fast.** Clear mornings can turn cloudy by afternoon, with rain lower down and snow higher up.
4. **Snow can be soft and deep after noon.** You may sink in on the way down. Gaiters help.
5. **Juda ka Talab may be thawing.** Don't step onto the ice in March; it can be thin.

## What is Kedarkantha summit day like in March?

The plan is the same as in winter: an early start, a steady climb and sunrise near the top. Because the sun rises earlier and is stronger in March, timing matters more. The snow is firm and easy to walk on before dawn, then softens quickly once the sun reaches it. By late morning, the descent can be soft, deep and slushy, and you may sink in up to your knees in places.

That's why your mountain guide will want to start on time and keep the group moving on the way down. Gaiters keep the wet snow out of your shoes, and poles help with balance in soft snow. Spring storms can still bring fresh snow overnight, so check the forecast and pack your warm layers whatever the calendar says.

## Who should do Kedarkantha in March?

Good for:

- People who want snow but dislike extreme cold
- First-timers who'd like a slightly gentler version of the trek
- Families with older children
- Trekkers who prefer quiet trails

Not ideal for:

- People who want deep snow all the way from Sankri
- Anyone hoping for perfectly stable weather; March can change quickly

## Is February or March better for Kedarkantha?

### Kedarkantha in February

- **Snow:** Deep, settled, all the way up from the forest
- **Cold:** Very cold
- **Snow texture:** Firm, especially in the morning
- **Crowds:** Low

### Kedarkantha in March

- **Snow:** Upper trail mostly, melting lower down
- **Cold:** Cold at night, mild in the day
- **Snow texture:** Firm early, slushy by afternoon
- **Crowds:** Low

If snow is the priority, choose February. If comfort matters more, choose March. See [Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in February?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-february) or the month-by-month guide in [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)

For the full overview, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide). March dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in April or May?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek in April and May: Snow and Weather
posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha in April and May: how much snow is left, the weather, crowds, the gear you need, and which of the two months suits you better.
posts.body:
April and May are the spring and early-summer months on Kedarkantha, and they suit people who want a softer, greener version of the trek. In April you usually still get snow on the upper slopes and near the summit, rhododendrons flowering in the forest, and nights that are cold but bearable. By May the snow has largely melted, the meadows turn green and the days are warm, so it becomes a pleasant forest-and-meadow walk with a summit view rather than a snow trek. Choose early April if you want a little snow; choose May if comfort and quiet trails matter more. Spring dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

Below is what each month is like on the trail: snow, weather, crowds, gear, and which of the two suits you better.

## How much snow is left on Kedarkantha in April and May?

It depends on how much fell in winter, and it changes week by week. As a rough guide:

### Kedarkantha in April

- **Lower trail and forest:** mostly clear. You walk on earth, roots and fallen leaves.
- **Around Juda ka Talab:** usually little or no snow, and the lake has thawed.
- **Base camp:** patches of snow, more in early April and after a heavy winter.
- **Summit approach:** snow in early April in most years, thinning through the month.

### Kedarkantha in May

- **Lower trail and Juda ka Talab:** no snow. The lake is open water.
- **Base camp:** usually green or brown meadow, sometimes with old snow in shaded hollows early in the month.
- **Summit:** often snow-free, or with small patches on the north-facing side.

Late snowfall still happens in April, especially in the first half, and a single storm can whiten the upper slopes for a few days. In May, plan as if there won't be snow and treat any you find as a bonus. Either way, check our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) before you book.

What you get in both months is snow in the distance. The big peaks around Kedarkantha keep their snow long after the trail has melted, so a clear summit morning still has plenty of white in it.

## What is the weather like on Kedarkantha in April and May?

Spring weather: pleasant days, cool to cold nights higher up, and clouds that build in the afternoon.

### April temperatures on the Kedarkantha trek

- **Sankri:** days 16°C to 22°C, nights 5°C to 9°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 10°C to 16°C, nights 0°C to 4°C
- **Base camp:** days 8°C to 14°C, nights −2°C to 2°C

### May temperatures on the Kedarkantha trek

- **Sankri:** days 20°C to 26°C, nights 9°C to 13°C
- **Juda ka Talab:** days 14°C to 20°C, nights 4°C to 8°C
- **Base camp:** days 12°C to 18°C, nights 1°C to 5°C

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

Mornings are usually the clearest time of day in both months. By early afternoon, clouds often build over the peaks, and a short shower or a little hail isn't unusual in April. In May, thunderstorms with rain or hail become more common towards the end of the month as the weather heads towards the monsoon. That's why groups walk early and aim to reach camp by lunchtime.

Summer haze can also soften the distant views in the second half of May. For the sharpest mountain views of the year, October and February are better ([Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)).

The upside is comfort. You can sit outside your tent in the evening without shivering, and you'll sleep far better than in winter.

## How crowded is Kedarkantha in April and May?

Both are among the quietest months on the trail.

- **April:** most winter trekkers have moved on, and summer treks elsewhere haven't fully started. Weekends are steady, weekdays calm. Easter, Ambedkar Jayanti or other long weekends can bring short spikes.
- **May:** few people think of Kedarkantha as a summer trek, and many head to higher treks that open around now. You'll usually share campsites with only a few groups.

On a weekday you may have the summit almost to yourselves. The road from Dehradun to Sankri, though, can be busy in May with holiday traffic heading to the hills, so leave early.

## What gear do you need for Kedarkantha in April and May?

You need less winter gear than in December or January, but you still need warmth for nights and summit morning.

Bring in both months:

- A fleece and a thermal for evenings and nights
- Quick-dry T-shirts (two or three) and light trekking pants for warm days
- A waterproof jacket or poncho for afternoon showers
- Trekking shoes with good grip; the forest trail can be slippery after rain
- Sun cap, SPF 50 sunscreen, lip balm and sunglasses (the sun is strong, and there may be glare off snow up high)
- Two water bottles; you'll drink more in warm weather

Extra for April:

- A padded jacket or a light down jacket (a −5°C rating is plenty)
- Two pairs of gloves: a light pair, and a warmer pair for summit morning

Extra for May:

- A light padded jacket is enough for evenings
- Insect repellent for the lower forest

You can usually leave behind the heavy −10°C down jacket, thick waterproof outer gloves and hand warmers. Microspikes are rarely needed after mid-April, though we carry them early in the month in case of icy patches. Gaiters aren't needed in May. The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list), and the general version in [What should you pack for a summer trek?](/blog/summer-trek-packing-list)

## What is the Kedarkantha trail like in spring?

The forest comes alive. Rhododendrons flower in shades of red and pink through the oak forest, usually around March and April depending on altitude and the year. Birds are much more active than in winter, and the forest is full of birdsong by May.

The meadows change colour. Early April can still look wintry above the treeline. By late April the slopes around base camp are mostly open grass, and in May they turn green, with the first wildflowers.

The walking is easier underfoot. Without deep snow, you move faster, and there's no hard ice to worry about. Summit day is still the longest day, with the same steep final climb ([How high is Kedarkantha peak, and how hard is summit day?](/blog/kedarkantha-height)).

The days are long. Daylight lasts well into the evening, so you get more time to relax at camp. In May your mountain guide may start summit day a little later than in winter, though an early start still gives the clearest view and keeps you ahead of afternoon storms.

## April or May: which month is better for Kedarkantha?

Choose April if:

- You'd like some snow near the summit, especially in the first half of the month
- You want rhododendrons in flower
- You're happy with cold, but not freezing, nights

Choose May if:

- You want the warmest, most comfortable version of the trek
- You don't mind a snow-free trail
- You're travelling in the school holidays, perhaps with family

If you want more snow than April usually gives, March is the better month ([Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in March?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-march)).

## Who should do Kedarkantha in April or May?

Good for:

- People who feel the cold badly but still want a Himalayan summit
- Families with younger trekkers, and older trekkers, who want a gentler version of the trek ([Can your parents do the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-with-parents))
- Nature lovers who enjoy flowers and birds
- Anyone escaping the heat of the plains who wants a quiet trail

Not ideal for:

- People whose main goal is walking through deep snow
- Photographers chasing the crisp, clear views of autumn and winter

## Should you pick another trek in May instead of Kedarkantha?

If you're free in May and want snow underfoot or bigger scenery, look at treks that open in late spring and summer, many of which go higher. Our lists of [Himalayan treks worth doing in summer](/blog/summer-treks-uttarakhand-himachal) and [treks in May](/blog/treks-in-may-uttarakhand-himachal) will help.

If you want a short, easy summit with a forest walk and you're happy without snow, Kedarkantha in May is a lovely, uncrowded choice.

## Tips for trekking Kedarkantha in spring

1. **Start each day early.** Clear mornings, firm ground and no afternoon storm to rush you.
2. Keep your rain layer at the top of your bag, not packed away.
3. **Use sunscreen every few hours.** Spring sun at altitude burns faster than you expect, even on cloudy days.
4. **Drink more than you think you need.** Warm days at altitude dry you out.
5. **Look after your feet.** Wet trails after rain mean wet socks; change into dry ones at camp.

The full trek overview is in [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide), and every month is compared in [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek) Spring dates are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: What should you know before the Kedarkantha trek?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek Tips: What to Know Before You Go
posts.excerpt: Practical things to know before the Kedarkantha trek, from what first-timers underestimate to trail rules and habits that help.
posts.body:
Before the Kedarkantha trek, the most useful things to know are simple. It's a real Himalayan winter trek, not a long walk. The summit day starts in the dark, and it's the hardest day by far. Nights at base camp go well below freezing. There's almost no phone signal after Sankri, and no ATM either. Get those four things right, train for a month and pack properly, and Kedarkantha is one of the most rewarding first treks in India.

This guide gathers what first-timers most often wish they'd been told: what people underestimate, what to sort out before you reach Sankri, the rules on the trail, and the small habits that make the trek easier. If you're still deciding on dates, start with [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek), and you can see our departures on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## What do first-timers underestimate about Kedarkantha?

The journey to Sankri. Most people plan for the trek and forget the road. Dehradun to Sankri takes about 9 to 10 hours on a winding mountain road, and the trek can't start until you've done it. Arriving tired, carsick and late makes day 2 much harder than it needs to be. Plan an overnight train or bus to Dehradun, leave early in the morning, and treat the drive as part of the trek ([How do you get from Dehradun to Sankri by bus, jeep or taxi?](/blog/dehradun-to-sankri)).

Summit day. On paper, Kedarkantha is 4 to 6 km a day. In reality, summit day is a pre-dawn start, a steep climb on snow, a few minutes at the top and a long descent, usually 7 to 8 hours in total. It's the day that decides whether you enjoy the trek, and it rewards people who trained for it ([How high is Kedarkantha peak, and how hard is summit day?](/blog/kedarkantha-height)).

The cold, especially at night. Daytime in the sun can feel pleasant even in January. Then the sun drops behind the ridge around 4 pm and the temperature falls fast. At base camp in December and January, nights are often −10°C or colder. The people who struggle are usually not underdressed during the day; they're the ones who let their clothes get damp and had nothing dry to change into at camp ([How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)).

Walking on snow. Snow changes the trek. Climbs feel longer, descents are slippery, and your legs work harder on every step. Good grip, microspikes when the trail is icy, and a slow, steady pace matter more than fitness alone ([How do you walk on snow without slipping?](/blog/walking-on-snow)).

Being out of reach. Signal fades soon after Sankri. For three days you won't be able to call home, check work email or send photos. Tell people in advance ([Is there mobile network on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-network)).

## What should you do before reaching Sankri for the Kedarkantha trek?

Most of the work for a good trek happens at home.

1. **Train for four to six weeks.** Build up to walking or jogging 5 km in under 40 minutes, climb stairs with a light backpack, and do one long walk every weekend. If you can't comfortably walk for five hours with breaks, summit day will be a struggle ([How do you train for a trek in four weeks?](/blog/4-week-trek-training-plan)).
2. **Break in your shoes.** Wear your trekking shoes for at least two weeks before the trek, on long walks and stairs. New shoes on a snow trek are the most common cause of blisters.
3. **Carry original ID.** The forest permit for the Govind area needs a government photo ID. Carry the original and a photocopy ([Do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-permit)).
4. **Withdraw enough cash.** There's no ATM in Sankri, and card or UPI payments often fail because of the network. Draw cash in Dehradun or on the way, enough for travel, food on the road, gear rental, and a buffer ([How much cash should you carry on a trek?](/blog/cash-on-trek)).
5. **Sort your gear.** Decide what you'll buy, borrow and rent. Big items like a down jacket can be rented in Sankri, but the best stock goes early in peak weeks ([Where can you rent trekking gear in Sankri?](/blog/rent-trekking-gear-sankri)). The full list is in [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list)
6. **Check your health.** If you have a medical condition, talk to your doctor about a trek to 12,500 ft before you book. A cold or fever just before departure is worth taking seriously too ([Can you trek with a medical condition?](/blog/trekking-with-medical-condition)).
7. **Take insurance.** Evacuation and hospital costs aren't covered by any trek fee. A policy that covers trekking up to about 4,000 m is worth having ([Do you really need trekking insurance in India?](/blog/trekking-insurance-india)).
8. **Check the snow and road before you leave.** Snow levels change week by week, and heavy snow or landslides can close the road to Sankri. Look at the latest conditions a few days before travel ([Is there snow on Kedarkantha right now?](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update)).

## Which rules apply on the Kedarkantha trail?

Kedarkantha lies inside the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park, so the forest department's rules apply, and so do the trek team's.

### Forest department rules for Kedarkantha

- You need a valid forest permit for every trekker, checked at the forest post in Sankri.
- **Camp only at designated campsites.** Camping rules on high meadows have tightened in Uttarakhand in recent years, and forest officials can change them ([Can you still camp on Uttarakhand's meadows?](/blog/uttarakhand-bugyal-camping-ban)).
- **No plastic left behind.** Carry out every wrapper, bottle and wet wipe. Some checkposts count plastic items going in and out.
- **No disturbing wildlife or plants.** Don't feed animals, pick flowers or break branches.

### Trek team rules on Kedarkantha

- **Your mountain guide decides when to turn back.** On summit day, weather or snow conditions may mean turning around before the top. That decision is final and it's there to bring everyone home.
- **Stay with the group.** Don't walk ahead out of sight or lag far behind, especially in snow or fog, when trails disappear quickly.
- **No alcohol or smoking.** Both make the cold and the altitude harder on your body, and both are against the rules on our treks.
- **No campfires.** Wood is scarce, and fires scar the campsites ([Why are campfires discouraged on Himalayan treks?](/blog/campfire-on-trek)).
- **Use the toilet tents.** Each camp has toilet tents with dry pits. Don't use the area around the lake or streams ([What are toilets like on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/toilets-on-trek)).

## Habits that make the Kedarkantha trek easier

These small things make a bigger difference than any piece of gear.

1. **Walk slower than you think you need to.** The first hour out of Sankri is steep. People who rush it pay for it on day 3.
2. **Drink water even when you're not thirsty.** Cold weather hides dehydration, and dehydration feels a lot like altitude sickness. Aim for 3 to 4 litres a day ([How much water should you drink on a trek?](/blog/how-much-water-to-drink-trekking)).
3. **Change into dry clothes as soon as you reach camp.** Sweat cools fast. Keep one set of thermals and socks only for camp and sleeping.
4. **Eat properly, even if you don't feel hungry.** Appetite drops with altitude, but your body needs fuel to stay warm.
5. Keep your water bottle and phone inside your sleeping bag on the coldest nights, so they don't freeze or die ([How do you keep phone batteries alive in the cold?](/blog/battery-drain-in-cold)).
6. Tell your mountain guide early if you have a headache, feel sick or can't feel your toes. Small problems are easy to fix; big ones aren't.
7. Use the toilet before you get into your sleeping bag. Getting out at 2 am at −10°C is miserable.
8. **Pack your daypack the night before summit day.** Headtorch, gloves, water, snacks and sunglasses, ready to grab in the dark.

## Things people often get wrong about Kedarkantha

- **Myth:** "It's an easy trek, I don't need to train." Fact: It's graded easy to moderate, but summit day is long and steep. Training makes it enjoyable.
- **Myth:** "I'll buy everything in Sankri." Fact: Rental stock is limited in peak weeks, and you can't buy proper trekking shoes there.
- **Myth:** "I'll call home from the summit." Fact: Signal is unreliable. Plan to be out of touch for three days.
- **Myth:** "Snow is guaranteed in December." Fact: Snow varies a lot from year to year. Early December can be thin.
- **Myth:** "The summit is the hard part, the descent is easy." Fact: The long descent on snow is where knees hurt and people slip. Poles help ([How do you walk downhill without hurting your knees?](/blog/walking-downhill-trek)).

## What should you know about Sankri, the Kedarkantha base village?

Sankri is a small village at the end of the road, and it's where your trek really begins.

- **It's busy in season.** In late December and January, guesthouses, gear shops and shared jeeps fill up. Book your stay in advance if you're arriving on your own ([Where should you stay in Sankri before a trek?](/blog/where-to-stay-in-sankri)).
- **Facilities are basic.** Expect simple rooms, bucket hot water and patchy electricity. That's part of the experience.
- **Arriving a day early helps.** An extra night lets you recover from the drive, rent gear calmly and walk around the village ([What can you do in Sankri if you arrive a day early?](/blog/things-to-do-in-sankri)).
- **It's people's home.** Ask before photographing people or houses, dress modestly and keep noise down at night ([What is Sankri village like?](/blog/sankri-village)).

## A Kedarkantha checklist for the week before you leave

Run through this list about a week before departure. It catches most of the small problems that spoil a trek.

- Confirm your departure date, pick-up point and time with your operator.
- Book or confirm your bus or train to Dehradun, both ways.
- Check the latest snow and weather on our [weekly Kedarkantha snow report](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update).
- Withdraw enough cash for the whole trip, plus a buffer for delays.
- Pack your bag and weigh it. Aim for 8 to 10 kg, and take things out if it's heavier.
- Pack your daypack separately with water bottles, snacks, a warm layer and your headtorch.
- Put your original ID and a photocopy in a waterproof pouch.
- Charge your phone, power bank and headtorch, and pack spare batteries.
- Download offline maps, music or books for the evenings.
- Pack your personal medicines for every day of the trip, plus a few spare days.
- Share your itinerary and your operator's phone number with family.
- Sleep well for the last few nights. Arriving tired makes the first climb harder.

## Where to read next about Kedarkantha

If you're new to trekking, read [How hard is the Kedarkantha trek for a beginner?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-difficulty) and the day-by-day plan in [How many days is the Kedarkantha trek, and what is the day-wise route?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-itinerary) For the full overview, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide)

When you're ready to book, our small groups of up to ten trekkers, each with a named mountain guide, are listed on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Height and Summit Day: How Hard Is It?
posts.excerpt: Kedarkantha's summit height, the pre-dawn start, how long summit day takes and what makes it hard in snow.
posts.body:
The Kedarkantha summit stands at about 12,500 ft (3,810 m). You reach it on the morning of day 4, after a pre-dawn start from base camp at about 11,250 ft. The climb itself gains roughly 1,250 ft and usually takes 3 to 4 hours, with the steepest section in the last hour. Then comes a long descent all the way to Juda ka Talab. In total, summit day is usually 7 to 8 hours of walking, and it's the hardest day of the trek.

Here's what the summit is like, how the day runs, and what makes it tough when the mountain is under snow. For the rest of the trek, see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## How high is Kedarkantha peak?

Kedarkantha's summit is usually given as 12,500 ft, or about 3,810 m. Published figures vary a little, from about 12,400 to 12,500 ft, depending on the source and the GPS used.

To put that in context:

- **Sankri, where you start:** 6,455 ft (1,967 m)
- **Juda ka Talab camp:** 8,860 ft (2,700 m)
- **Kedarkantha base camp:** 11,250 ft (3,430 m)
- **Summit:** 12,500 ft (3,810 m)

So over the trek you climb about 6,000 ft from Sankri, but only about 1,250 ft on summit morning itself. The height is spread over three days, which is why most people adjust to it well ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).

The summit is a small, rounded top with a little shrine of stones and flags. From it, on a clear morning, you look out over the peaks of the Garhwal Himalaya. Which ones you can name is in [Which peaks can you see from the Kedarkantha summit?](/blog/kedarkantha-summit-view)

## What time does Kedarkantha summit day start?

Summit day starts early, usually with a wake-up around 2:30 to 3 am and walking by 3:30 to 4 am. There are three reasons for starting in the dark:

1. **To reach the top for sunrise.** The views are clearest in the early morning, before clouds build up.
2. **Snow is firmer before the sun hits it.** Frozen snow is easier and safer to walk on than soft, slushy snow later in the day.
3. **Afternoon weather.** If the weather turns, it usually does so after midday. An early start gives you time to get down.

You'll walk by headtorch, in a line behind your mountain guide, in your warmest layers. In the busiest weeks, many groups set off within the same hour, so the trail can look like a long line of lights. A small group can time its start to avoid the worst of it. It's the coldest part of the whole trek, often well below −10°C with wind. More on why early starts matter is in [Why do summit climbs start before dawn?](/blog/why-summit-start-early)

## How long does the Kedarkantha summit climb take, up and down?

- **Base camp to the summit ridge (2 to 3 hours):** Steady climb on snow, mostly open slopes.
- **Ridge to the summit (45 minutes to 1 hour):** The steepest part of the trek.
- **Time at the top (20 to 40 minutes):** Sunrise, photos, a hot drink if the weather allows.
- **Summit back to base camp (1.5 to 2 hours):** Steep descent on snow; slow and careful.
- **Base camp to Juda ka Talab (2 to 3 hours):** Long descent into the forest.
- **Total (7 to 8 hours):** About 6 km of walking.

The times depend on snow, weather and the group. Fresh deep snow can add an hour or more. A small group can keep a steady rhythm without long waits, which helps ([Is a small trek group better than a big one?](/blog/small-group-trek)).

Some operators descend to a different camp such as Hargaon instead of Juda ka Talab. The effort is similar either way ([Which route is best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-route)).

## What makes the Kedarkantha summit tough in snow?

The steep final section. The last hour before the top is the steepest part of the trek. In deep snow it means kicking steps and using your poles for balance. In icy conditions it means microspikes and short, careful steps.

Cold, dark and wind together. You start in the coldest hour of the night, often with wind on the open slopes. Cold hands make it hard to use poles and zips, so warm gloves and a spare pair matter ([Which gloves and socks keep you warm on a snow trek?](/blog/gloves-for-snow-trek)).

Thin air. At 12,500 ft there's noticeably less oxygen. Most people feel breathless on the climb and need to stop more often. Slow, steady steps work better than bursts of speed.

The descent. Coming down on snow is harder than going up for many people. Legs are tired, the slope is steep and slipping is easy. This is where knees ache and falls happen ([How do you walk downhill without hurting your knees?](/blog/walking-downhill-trek)).

The length of the day. After the summit, you still have several hours of walking down to Juda ka Talab. Pacing yourself on the way up leaves energy for the way down.

## How do you make Kedarkantha summit day easier?

- **Train for it.** One long walk each weekend for a month, ideally with stairs or hills, makes the biggest difference ([How do you train for a trek in four weeks?](/blog/4-week-trek-training-plan)).
- **Sleep and eat well the day before.** Eat a full dinner and drink plenty of water, even if you're not hungry.
- **Pack your daypack the night before.** Headtorch, spare batteries, water, snacks, gloves, a warm layer and sunglasses.
- **Wear the right shoes.** Good grip and ankle support, with microspikes on icy days ([Do you need microspikes or crampons on a trek?](/blog/microspikes-for-trekking)).
- **Use trekking poles.** They take strain off your legs on the climb and your knees on the descent.
- **Listen to your mountain guide.** If conditions are unsafe, the group turns back. That's part of the plan, not a failure.

## What can you see from the top of Kedarkantha?

On a clear morning you get a view in almost every direction. The peaks people most often point out are the Swargarohini group, Bandarpoonch and its dark neighbour Kalanag (also called Black Peak), and Ranglana, with the ranges around Yamunotri and Gangotri further away and the Har Ki Dun valley below. The view is usually clearest in the first hour after sunrise, before clouds build.

The summit is also a sacred spot for the villages below. You'll usually find a small stone shrine to Lord Shiva with a trishul (trident) and offerings left by local people. Don't climb on it, move anything or leave litter near it. Every peak is labelled in [Which peaks can you see from the Kedarkantha summit?](/blog/kedarkantha-summit-view)

## What should you carry on Kedarkantha summit day?

You leave your main bag at base camp, so only carry a light daypack, but make sure it has these:

- Your warmest layers: down jacket, windproof shell, balaclava, and liner gloves under outer gloves
- One to one and a half litres of warm water in an insulated bottle, so it doesn't freeze
- Snacks you can eat with gloves on: dry fruit, chocolate, energy bars
- Headtorch with spare batteries, kept warm in an inside pocket
- Sunglasses and sunscreen for the descent, when the sun is on the snow
- Microspikes and trekking poles in winter
- Your phone in an inside pocket, so the cold doesn't drain it before the top
- Any personal medicines

Everything else stays in the tent. A lighter pack makes the steep final climb noticeably easier.

## How does Kedarkantha's height compare with other beginner summits?

At about 12,500 ft, Kedarkantha is one of the highest summits a beginner can reach in winter in Uttarakhand. For comparison, using commonly published figures:

- **Nag Tibba:** about 9,900 ft. A shorter, lower weekend trek.
- **Dayara Bugyal:** about 12,000 ft at the top of the meadows. Gentler slopes, no summit cone.
- **Brahmatal:** about 12,250 ft. Similar height, with a summit-style finish.
- **Chandrashila, above Tungnath:** about 13,000 ft. Higher, but reached by a short, steep climb from a road-accessible area.

What makes Kedarkantha special is the combination: a real summit, at a good height, reached over three gentle days, with snow from December to March.

## What happens if the Kedarkantha summit is called off?

Sometimes heavy snow, strong wind or poor visibility makes the summit unsafe. In that case your mountain guide may delay the start, turn back partway, or skip the summit and descend. If your trek has a spare day, it may be possible to try again. Safety decides, not the plan.

For how the whole trek fits together, see [How hard is the Kedarkantha trek for a beginner?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-difficulty) and [How many days is the Kedarkantha trek, and what is the day-wise route?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-itinerary) Dates for our small-group departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.excerpt: The different routes to the Kedarkantha summit, how they compare and which one suits you.
posts.body:
For most people, the best route to Kedarkantha is the classic one from Sankri, through Juda ka Talab to base camp and the summit. It has the gentlest climbs, the best-known campsites, easy access by road and the most support if something goes wrong. Two quieter routes, from Kotgaon and from Gaichawan Gaon, reach the same summit from other sides. They're steeper and less used, which suits experienced trekkers who want fewer people around. There's also a common variation that comes down from the summit through Hargaon.

Here's how the routes compare, which one suits a beginner, and which is quietest. Our departures use the Sankri route; details are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Which routes lead to the Kedarkantha summit?

Kedarkantha rises above several valleys, so more than one trail leads up it. The four you'll hear about:

1. **The Sankri route (the classic).** Sankri → Juda ka Talab → Kedarkantha base camp → summit → back to Juda ka Talab → Sankri. You walk straight out of the village, climb through pine and oak forest to the lake at Juda ka Talab, then above the treeline to base camp. This is the route almost every first-timer takes.
2. **The Sankri route with a Hargaon descent.** The way up is the same, but after the summit you descend by a different trail to a campsite at Hargaon, then walk down to Sankri the next day. It's a loop rather than an out-and-back, so you see new forest on the way down.
3. **The Kotgaon route.** Starts from the village of Kotgaon, near Sankri on the road from Mori. The trail climbs to campsites usually named Khujaai and Bhoja Dhadi (about 9,450 ft and 10,700 ft) before joining the summit approach. Fewer groups use it.
4. **The Gaichawan Gaon route.** Starts from Gaichawan village, lower down at about 5,600 ft, and climbs through campsites commonly named Julota and Pukhrola. It's the longest climb of the four and the least used.

**Note:** Route names, campsites and altitudes for the less-used routes vary between sources.

## How do the Kedarkantha routes differ in length and climb?

### The Sankri route via Juda ka Talab

- **Start altitude:** About 6,455 ft
- **Days on foot:** 4
- **Gradient:** Gentle to moderate, steep only near the top
- **Crowds:** Busy in winter
- **Road access:** Easy; buses and jeeps reach Sankri

### The Sankri route with a Hargaon descent

- **Start altitude:** About 6,455 ft
- **Days on foot:** 4
- **Gradient:** Similar to the classic
- **Crowds:** Busy going up, quieter coming down
- **Road access:** Easy

### The Kotgaon route

- **Start altitude:** About 6,400 ft
- **Days on foot:** 4 to 5
- **Gradient:** Steeper than Sankri
- **Crowds:** Quiet
- **Road access:** Short drive from Sankri side

### The Gaichawan Gaon route

- **Start altitude:** About 5,600 ft
- **Days on foot:** 4 to 5
- **Gradient:** Steeper and longer
- **Crowds:** Very quiet
- **Road access:** Fewer transport options

**Note:** Days and gradients are typical.

The main difference is how the height is spread out. On the Sankri route, the climb is split into three manageable days, with the steep bit saved for summit morning. On the Kotgaon and Gaichawan routes, you gain more height on some days, and the trails are rougher because fewer people walk them.

## Which Kedarkantha route suits beginners?

The Sankri route, without much doubt. For a first trek it has clear advantages:

- **The gentlest gradient.** You gain height steadily over three days, which helps your body adjust to the altitude ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).
- **Well-marked trail.** In snow, a trail that many people walk is easier to follow and pack down.
- **Easy access.** Sankri has guesthouses, gear rental and transport, so you start rested and fully equipped ([Where should you stay in Sankri before a trek?](/blog/where-to-stay-in-sankri)).
- **More help nearby.** If someone needs to come down, the way back to Sankri is short and well known.

The Hargaon descent is also fine for beginners, provided the snow conditions on that side are safe. Your mountain guide decides on the day.

The Kotgaon and Gaichawan routes are better left for a second or third trek, or for trekkers who are fit, comfortable on rough ground and trekking with a mountain guide who knows that side well.

## Which Kedarkantha route is quieter?

The Kotgaon and Gaichawan Gaon routes are far quieter. On many days you may not meet another group.

The Sankri route is busy, especially in late December and early January. On peak nights, Juda ka Talab can host a large number of tents. If you'd like the classic route with fewer people, a few choices help:

1. Go on a weekday start, so your summit doesn't fall on a weekend.
2. Avoid the Christmas to New Year week, the busiest stretch of the season.
3. Pick February or March, when crowds thin and snow is still good ([Is the Kedarkantha trek worth doing in February?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-in-february)).
4. Join a small group. A group of up to ten moves more freely and can time its walking to avoid the busiest stretches ([Is a small trek group better than a big one?](/blog/small-group-trek)).

Because of the crowds, some large trekking companies have moved their groups off the Sankri route altogether and now start from Kotgaon or Gaichawan Gaon instead. The two sides also feel different in winter. On the Kotgaon side, the peak itself blocks the morning and evening sun, so camps get only a few hours of sunlight around midday; it's colder, and snow lingers longer. The Gaichawan Gaon side faces west and gets sun from early morning, so camps there feel warmer. Campsite names on these routes also differ between operators, so ask exactly where you'll sleep.

More on crowding is in [Is overcrowding ruining popular treks like Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-crowded)

## Which Kedarkantha route do we use, and why?

We run Kedarkantha on the Sankri route, out and back through Juda ka Talab: five days from Sankri to Sankri, with base camp at about 11,250 ft and the summit on day 4. It's the safest choice for mixed groups of first-timers and the route our mountain guides know best in every kind of snow. The day-by-day plan is in [How many days is the Kedarkantha trek, and what is the day-wise route?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-itinerary)

## What does each Kedarkantha route look like on the ground?

Sankri route. The first hour climbs steeply through the village fields and into the forest. Then the trail settles into a steady zigzag through pine and oak, with the snow getting deeper as you climb. Juda ka Talab appears suddenly in a clearing. Above it, the forest thins, rhododendron and birch give way to open slopes, and base camp sits on a wide shoulder with the summit cone right above you. The final climb is the steepest part, on open snow with views opening up in every direction.

Hargaon descent. From the summit, instead of retracing your steps, you drop down a different ridge into forest on the far side and camp at Hargaon, a clearing lower down. The trail is less trampled than the main one, so in fresh snow it can be slower and harder to follow. It's a nice change of scenery, but it depends more on a mountain guide who knows that side well.

Kotgaon and Gaichawan Gaon. Both start lower, among village fields and terraces, and climb through thicker, quieter forest with fewer marked paths. You see more village life at the start and almost no other groups higher up. The trade-off is steeper ground, rougher trails and fewer people around if something goes wrong.

## How do you reach the start of each Kedarkantha route?

All four routes begin in the same corner of Uttarkashi district, so the journey from Dehradun is almost the same: about 9 to 10 hours by road through Mussoorie, Purola and Mori.

- **Sankri route and Hargaon descent:** start in Sankri itself, the end of the road for buses and shared jeeps from Dehradun. Most guesthouses, rental shops and local guides are here.
- **Kotgaon route:** starts from Kotgaon village, a short drive from the Sankri side of the valley.
- **Gaichawan Gaon route:** starts from Gaichawan Gaon, only a few kilometres from Sankri by road, with Haltwad usually named as the last road head.

Whichever route you choose, the whole area lies inside the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park, so every trekker needs a forest permit, normally issued at the checkpost in Sankri ([Do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-permit)). Transport options are in [How do you get from Dehradun to Sankri by bus, jeep or taxi?](/blog/dehradun-to-sankri)

## Can you combine Kedarkantha routes?

Yes, and some groups do. The most common combination is up from Sankri through Juda ka Talab and down through Hargaon, which turns the trek into a loop. Fit, experienced groups sometimes go up from Kotgaon and come down to Sankri. Combinations need the right permits and good knowledge of both sides, and they work best outside the deepest snow of January. For a first trek, keep it simple: up and down the Sankri route.

## A word on Kedarkantha short cuts and "two-day" versions

You'll see offers to do Kedarkantha in fewer days by skipping a camp. We don't recommend it for most people. Gaining 6,000 ft in two days raises the risk of altitude sickness, makes summit day much harder, and leaves no time to wait out bad weather. Five days from Sankri is the comfortable minimum for a first-timer.

For the full picture, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide), or check dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is Juda ka Talab on the Kedarkantha trek frozen in winter?
posts.seo_title: Juda ka Talab, Kedarkantha: When Does It Freeze?
posts.excerpt: Juda ka Talab on the Kedarkantha trail: when it freezes, whether it is safe to step on and the story behind it.
posts.body:
Yes, in deep winter Juda ka Talab usually freezes over. The lake, at about 8,860 ft on the Kedarkantha trail, typically starts to ice at the edges in December and freezes across in the coldest weeks of late December, January and early February. By March it thaws again. Even when it looks solid, don't walk on it. The ice thickness varies, there's no way to check it safely, and a fall through into freezing water is a real emergency.

Here's where the lake is, when it freezes, why you should stay off the ice, and the legend that gives it its name. For the trek it sits on, see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Where is Juda ka Talab on the Kedarkantha trek?

Juda ka Talab is a small lake in a forest clearing about 4 km above Sankri, on the main route to Kedarkantha. It's the first campsite on the trek, reached on day 2 after a 4 to 5 hour climb through pine and oak forest.

- **Altitude:** About 8,860 ft (2,700 m)
- **Distance from Sankri:** About 4 km on foot
- **Time from Sankri:** 4 to 5 hours
- **Role on the trek:** First camp; most groups also sleep here again on the way down
- **Surroundings:** Tall pine and oak forest, with open clearings for tents

The lake is small. You can walk around it in a few minutes. What makes it special is the setting: a ring of tall trees, the first snow you meet on the trek, and in winter a sheet of ice that turns the clearing quiet and white.

Because it's the first camp, Juda ka Talab is also where many trekkers spend their first night in a tent. More on what the camp is like is in [What are the campsites on the Kedarkantha trek like?](/blog/kedarkantha-campsites)

## When does Juda ka Talab freeze, and for how long?

The freeze depends on how cold and snowy the winter is. A typical pattern:

- **November:** Open water, frost on the edges on cold mornings
- **Early December:** Ice forming at the edges, thin skin of ice on very cold nights
- **Late December:** Often frozen across, sometimes under snow
- **January:** Usually frozen solid, often covered in snow
- **February:** Usually frozen, starting to soften late in the month
- **March:** Thawing; patches of ice, then open water
- **April:** Open water, snow gone from the clearing in most years

**Note:** Typical pattern only. A mild winter can leave the lake open for much of December, and a cold one can freeze it earlier.

If seeing the frozen lake matters to you, late December to early February is your best window. Check our [Kedarkantha snow update](/blog/kedarkantha-snow-update) before you travel, as it notes whether the lake has frozen. To choose your month, see [Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)

## Is it safe to walk on frozen Juda ka Talab?

No. Even in January, when the lake looks solid and people are photographed standing on it, we strongly advise against stepping onto the ice.

1. **You can't see how thick the ice is.** Ice is often thinner near the edges, where streams flow in and where the sun hits it.
2. **Snow hides weak spots.** A layer of snow insulates the ice and can keep it thinner than it looks.
3. **Falling through is an emergency.** The water is near freezing. Wet clothes at −5°C to −10°C quickly lead to hypothermia, and you're hours from a road ([What is hypothermia and how do you spot it on a trek?](/blog/hypothermia-trekking)).
4. **It's a water source and a sacred place.** The lake matters to local people, and trampling it doesn't help.

Take your photos from the edge. The lake looks better from the bank anyway, with the trees reflected or the snow untouched.

## What is the story behind Juda ka Talab?

The name means, roughly, "the lake of the jata", the matted hair of Lord Shiva. The story told in the area is that Shiva was meditating in these mountains, and as he moved, a lock of his hair fell here and formed the lake.

You'll hear other versions too. One says there were once two small pools here that joined into one lake, and that "juda" refers to this joining. Another says the lake feeds the streams that flow out underground lower down the hill.

It's tied to a wider set of legends in the valley. Kedarkantha itself is linked to Shiva, and many people in the villages around Sankri see the mountain as sacred. You'll find small shrines along the way. Please treat them with respect: don't climb on them, move offerings or leave litter nearby ([How should you respect local culture while trekking?](/blog/respect-local-culture-trek)). For the story behind the mountain's name, see [How did Kedarkantha get its name?](/blog/kedarkantha-name-meaning)

## How do you photograph Juda ka Talab?

The lake is small, so the best photos usually include the forest around it.

- **Go early or late.** Soft light in the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset makes the snow and trees glow. At midday, snow looks flat and grey in photos.
- **Shoot from the bank.** In winter, untouched snow on the ice looks far better than footprints, and it keeps you safely off the ice.
- **Look for reflections in spring and autumn.** On a still morning in October, November or April, the trees reflect in the open water.
- **Keep batteries warm.** Cold drains phone and camera batteries fast; carry a spare in an inside pocket.
- **Check before flying a drone.** The lake is inside a protected area, and drones may need permission from the forest department.

## What wildlife and plants can you see around Juda ka Talab?

Juda ka Talab sits in mixed forest of pine, oak and other broadleaf trees, inside the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary. In winter, the forest is quiet, but you'll often see tracks in the snow around camp: foxes, martens and sometimes deer. Birds are easier to spot in spring, when tits, woodpeckers and pheasants move through the trees, and you may hear the call of the Himalayan monal higher up.

Please keep the clearing clean for the animals as well as for other trekkers: no food scraps, no rubbish, and no washing in the lake. More on the sanctuary's animals is in [Which animals live in the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary?](/blog/govind-wildlife-sanctuary-animals)

## What is it like to camp at Juda ka Talab on the Kedarkantha trek?

- **Cold but sheltered.** The forest shields the camp from much of the wind, so it often feels warmer than base camp even on cold nights. In January, nights can still fall well below freezing ([How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)).
- **Busy in peak weeks.** It's the most crowded camp on the trek around Christmas and New Year. Weekday starts help.
- **Water.** In deep winter, when streams freeze, the trek team melts snow or carries water for cooking and drinking ([How do you stop water from freezing on a winter trek?](/blog/water-freezing-on-winter-trek)).
- **Leave no trace.** The clearing is small and gets heavy use. Carry out everything you bring in ([What does Leave No Trace mean on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/leave-no-trace)).

For the whole trek, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide), or see dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).
