posts.title: Do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Permit: Fees, Documents and Rules
posts.excerpt: What the Kedarkantha forest permit costs, where you get it in Sankri, which documents to carry and whether you need a guide.
posts.body:
Yes, you need a forest permit for the Kedarkantha trek. The trail lies inside the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park (also called Govind Pashu Vihar), so every trekker needs an entry permit from the forest department. You get it at the forest checkpost in Sankri, with a government photo ID. Recently reported fees are about ₹150 per Indian trekker for the first three days and about ₹600 for foreign nationals. Several recent sources also say the forest office issues permits only to groups with a registered local guide.

If you trek with an operator, the permit is usually arranged for you and included in the fee. On our departures it is; see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Why do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?

Kedarkantha, Har Ki Dun and the other treks around Sankri sit inside a protected area. The permit does three things:

- **Counts who is on the mountain.** If someone goes missing or needs help, the forest office knows who entered and when.
- **Funds the protected area.** Entry fees go to the forest department that manages the sanctuary.
- **Controls camping and waste.** Permits come with rules about where you can camp and what you must carry out.

The rules for the whole area are explained in [How do forest permits work for Uttarakhand treks?](/blog/uttarakhand-trekking-permit), and the bigger picture for India in [Do you need a permit for Himalayan treks in India?](/blog/trekking-permit-india)

## Which office issues the Kedarkantha permit?

Permits for Kedarkantha are issued at the forest checkpost in Sankri, close to where the trail leaves the village. One recent source gives the opening hours as about 7 am to 3 pm daily, which suits an early-morning start if you arrive the day before.

- **Where:** Forest checkpost, Sankri
- **Who issues it:** Uttarakhand Forest Department, Govind Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park
- **Fee, Indian nationals:** About ₹150 per person for the first three days
- **Fee, foreign nationals:** About ₹600 per person for the first three days, though some operators quote higher figures, so check the current rate
- **Extra days:** Charged per day beyond the first three
- **Camping fees:** May be charged per tent or per person per night

**Note:** Fees change, and published figures differ between sources. Treat these as a guide and confirm at the checkpost or with the forest office before you go.

If you're trekking with an operator, the team handles this the evening before or the morning of day 2. You just hand over your ID.

## Can you get the Kedarkantha permit online?

Some sources report that Indian nationals can apply online through the Uttarakhand Forest Department a few days in advance. In practice, most trekkers still get their permit at the Sankri checkpost, either directly or through their operator.

If you plan to apply online:

1. Apply at least three days before your trek.
2. Have scans of each trekker's photo ID ready.
3. Print or save the permit, and carry the original IDs; the checkpost may still want to see them.

## What documents do you need for the Kedarkantha permit?

- **Original government photo ID for every trekker.** Aadhaar, passport, driving licence and voter ID are the usual options.
- **A photocopy of the same ID.** Handy if the checkpost or your operator needs to keep a copy.
- Passport and visa for foreign nationals.
- **Medical certificate.** Not usually asked for at the checkpost, but many operators ask for a fitness declaration or certificate ([Do you need a medical certificate for a high-altitude trek?](/blog/medical-certificate-for-trekking)).

Keep your ID in a waterproof pouch in your daypack. You may be asked for it again on the way out. More on what to carry is in [What documents should you carry on a trek in India?](/blog/documents-for-trekking)

## Do you need a guide to get the Kedarkantha permit?

Several recent sources say the forest department issues Kedarkantha permits only when you're accompanied by a local guide registered with the forest department. Rules like this have tightened across Uttarakhand's protected areas in recent years.

What this means in practice:

- **With an operator:** nothing to do. Your mountain guide and the team handle it.
- **On your own:** expect to hire a registered local guide in Sankri before you can get a permit. Read [Can you do the Kedarkantha trek without a guide or agency?](/blog/kedarkantha-without-guide) and [How do you hire a local guide in Sankri safely?](/blog/local-guide-sankri)

## Rules that come with the Kedarkantha permit

- **Camp only at permitted campsites.** On the main route that means Juda ka Talab and base camp, unless the forest office says otherwise.
- **Carry out all waste, especially plastic.** Some checkposts in Uttarakhand note the plastic items you take in and check them on the way out.
- No fires for warmth or cooking with wood from the forest.
- No harming wildlife or plants.
- **Stick to your permitted dates.** If you stay longer, you may need to pay for the extra days.

Breaking these rules can lead to fines, and it makes life harder for everyone who treks here after you ([What does Leave No Trace mean on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/leave-no-trace)).

## What happens at the Sankri forest checkpost?

If you're with an operator, it usually takes a few minutes. Your mountain guide or team leader hands over the group list and IDs, pays the fees and collects the permit. The forest staff may count the group, check names against IDs and remind you of the rules, especially about waste. Keep your ID handy and be patient in peak weeks, when many groups pass through on the same morning. If you're arranging the permit yourself, arrive when the post opens so the paperwork doesn't delay your start, and bring exact cash, as card and UPI payments may not work.

## What if you stay longer, or combine Kedarkantha with another trek?

The fee is usually set for a fixed number of days, with extra days charged separately. If bad weather keeps you in the sanctuary for an extra night, the team sorts out the difference on the way out.

Many trekkers come back to the Sankri area for Har Ki Dun or Phulara Ridge, which lie in the same protected area. Each trek needs its own entry, so don't assume a Kedarkantha permit covers another trail. Some protected areas in India also charge separately for professional cameras or filming; check at the checkpost if you're carrying more than a phone or a small camera.

## Common Kedarkantha permit mistakes to avoid

- **Leaving your original ID at home.** A photo on your phone may not be accepted.
- **Arriving after the checkpost closes.** Reach Sankri in daylight so there's time to sort permits the same evening or early next morning.
- **Assuming you can book online.** As far as recent reports go, the permit is issued in person at Sankri.
- **Forgetting photocopies.** Carry a copy of your ID in case the checkpost or your operator needs to keep one.
- Foreign nationals travelling without a passport and valid visa. Both are needed, and the fee is higher.
- **Not counting your plastic.** If the checkpost logs plastic items going in, bring every one back out.

## Kedarkantha permits on our treks

On our Kedarkantha departures, the forest permit and entry fees are included in the trek fee, at Indian-national rates. Bring your original ID, and we'll take care of the rest. Foreign nationals pay the difference in fees. Dates and seats left are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha), and the full cost picture is in [How much does the Kedarkantha trek cost in total?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-cost)

posts.title: Can you do the Kedarkantha trek without a guide or agency?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Without a Guide: Is It Allowed?
posts.excerpt: Can you trek Kedarkantha on your own? The forest rules, what going independently involves and how to hire a registered local guide.
posts.body:
You can do Kedarkantha without a trekking company, but in practice you can't do it without a guide. Several recent sources say the forest department in Sankri issues permits only to trekkers accompanied by a registered local guide. So "going independent" on Kedarkantha usually means hiring your own local guide, and often a cook, porters or mules, and organising tents, food and safety yourself. It can save some money, but it puts all the planning and the winter risk on you.

This guide explains what's allowed, what an independent trek involves, the real risks in winter, and how to hire a reliable local guide in Sankri. If you'd rather have it all arranged, our small-group departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Is it allowed to do Kedarkantha without a guide?

Without an agency: yes. Nothing requires you to book through a trekking company. Plenty of trekkers organise Kedarkantha themselves.

Without any guide: generally no. Recent reports say the forest office at the Sankri checkpost will only issue Kedarkantha permits when you're accompanied by a local guide registered with the forest department. Rules in Uttarakhand's protected areas have tightened in recent years, and they're enforced at the checkpost.

The permit process and fees are explained in [Do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-permit), and the wider question in [Can you do a Himalayan trek without a trekking company?](/blog/trek-without-agency)

## What does an independent Kedarkantha trek involve?

If you go without an operator, you're responsible for everything an operator would normally handle:

- **Registered local guide:** Hire in Sankri, ideally booked in advance
- **Forest permit:** At the Sankri checkpost, with your guide
- **Tents, sleeping bags, mattresses:** Rent in Sankri or bring your own; all rated for winter
- **Kitchen kit, stove and fuel:** Rent in Sankri or hire a cook who brings it
- **Food for four days:** Buy in Dehradun or Sankri; plan meals and quantities
- **Carrying the load:** Porters or mules, hired in Sankri
- **Toilet arrangements:** Toilet tent and trowel; dig and fill pits
- **Safety kit:** First aid kit, microspikes, headtorches; oximeter recommended
- **Communication:** No signal above Sankri; plan check-in times and an emergency plan

Recently reported local rates in Sankri are roughly ₹1,000 a day for a local guide, ₹1,000 for a cook, ₹800 for a porter and ₹700 for a mule, plus their food and shelter. Porters typically carry about 20 kg and a mule about 40 kg, so even a small group needs a mule or two for tents, food and fuel. Your staff also need meals and a place to sleep at every camp, usually in the kitchen tent, so plan rations for them too.

For a group of three or four sharing costs, this can work out a little cheaper than an organised trek. For one or two people, it often costs about the same or more once you add up gear rental, food and staff ([How much does the Kedarkantha trek cost in total?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-cost)).

## What are the risks of an independent Kedarkantha trek in winter?

Kedarkantha in winter is a snow trek, and that changes what can go wrong.

1. **Losing the trail.** Fresh snow covers the path, especially above Juda ka Talab and on the summit slopes. In fog or a whiteout, open slopes look the same in every direction. A local guide who knows the mountain is your best protection ([What should you do if you get lost on a trek?](/blog/lost-on-trek)).
2. **Slips and falls on ice.** Icy patches on the descent are where most injuries happen. You need microspikes, poles and the judgement to know when to turn back ([Do you need microspikes or crampons on a trek?](/blog/microspikes-for-trekking)).
3. **Cold injuries.** Nights at base camp are often −10°C or colder. With rented, poorly rated sleeping bags, wet clothes or a bad tent pitch, mild discomfort can turn into hypothermia or frostnip ([What is hypothermia and how do you spot it on a trek?](/blog/hypothermia-trekking)).
4. **Altitude sickness with no one to spot it.** In a small independent group, nobody may be watching for early signs, and nobody carries oxygen or an oximeter ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).
5. **No way to call for help.** There's little or no mobile signal on the trail. If someone is hurt, the guide or a companion has to walk down for help, which takes hours ([What happens in a medical emergency on a remote trek?](/blog/emergency-on-trek)).
6. **Weather decisions.** Knowing when to delay or abandon the summit is the single most important safety call on Kedarkantha. Without an experienced mountain guide, groups tend to push on when they shouldn't.

None of this means an independent trek is reckless. It means the planning, kit and judgement that an operator provides become your job. If you're new to Himalayan winter trekking, we'd suggest doing your first one with an experienced team.

## How do you hire a local guide in Sankri for Kedarkantha?

1. **Book ahead in peak season.** Late December and January are busy. Good guides are often booked weeks in advance.
2. **Check registration.** Ask whether the guide is registered with the forest department, and confirm at the checkpost.
3. **Ask about winter experience.** How many times have they led Kedarkantha in deep snow? Have they turned a group back before, and why?
4. **Ask what they carry.** First aid kit, microspikes, rope, a way to call for help in an emergency.
5. **Agree the plan in writing.** Daily rate, number of days, food and shelter for staff, who carries what, and what happens if weather forces an extra day.
6. **Agree who decides on safety.** The guide should have the final word on turning back.

The checklist in full is in [How do you hire a local guide in Sankri safely?](/blog/local-guide-sankri), and how to check certificates is in [How can you check a trek guide's certificates?](/blog/verify-trek-guide-certification)

## What does an independent Kedarkantha trek cost compared with a group?

Here's a rough worked example for four friends doing the classic four walking days, using recently reported Sankri rates:

- **Local guide:** about ₹1,000 a day for four days, about ₹4,000
- **Cook:** about ₹1,000 a day for four days, about ₹4,000
- **Two mules for tents, food and fuel:** about ₹700 each a day, about ₹5,600
- Tents, sleeping bags, mattresses and kitchen kit, rented: roughly ₹6,000 to ₹8,000
- **Food for the group and staff:** roughly ₹4,000 to ₹6,000
- **Forest permits:** a few hundred rupees per person

That comes to roughly ₹24,000 to ₹28,000 for the group, or about ₹6,000 to ₹7,000 each, before travel, gear for yourself and any extra day. For two people the same fixed costs are split two ways, so it's closer to ₹10,000 to ₹12,000 each.

So going independent can be cheaper for a group of four or more, and rarely for one or two. What the numbers don't include is the safety kit an experienced operator carries, such as oxygen, an oximeter and a stretcher, or someone else handling the planning when the weather turns ([How much does the Kedarkantha trek cost in total?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-cost)).

## What to check before you go independent on Kedarkantha

- Your guide is registered and the forest office will issue your permit with them.
- Your guide has led Kedarkantha in deep snow, recently.
- Sleeping bags are rated for the nights you'll face, around −10°C in winter, and tents are four-season.
- You have enough stove fuel, plus a spare, and a way to melt snow for water.
- Your group carries a first aid kit and knows how to use it.
- Someone at home knows your route and your expected return time.
- You've checked the forecast and agreed a turnaround time for summit day.
- Everyone has insurance that covers trekking and evacuation.

## Independent or with a group: which Kedarkantha trek is right for you?

Going independent suits you if you've done winter treks before, you're in a group of three or more, you're comfortable organising gear and food, and you're happy to hire a reliable local guide.

Joining an organised trek suits you if it's your first Himalayan or snow trek, you're travelling alone or as a pair, or you'd rather spend your energy on the walk than on logistics. On our departures, groups are capped at ten, with a named mountain guide, oxygen, an oximeter and a full medical kit ([Is a small trek group better than a big one?](/blog/small-group-trek)).

If you're a solo traveller wondering how to join a group, see [Can you trek Kedarkantha solo?](/blog/kedarkantha-solo), and for the safety side of walking alone, [Is it safe to trek alone in winter near Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-solo) Dates for our departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Which Decathlon down jacket is warm enough for Kedarkantha?
posts.seo_title: Decathlon Jacket for Kedarkantha: Which One?
posts.excerpt: Which Decathlon jacket ratings work on Kedarkantha in December and January, and how to layer so a mid-range jacket is enough.
posts.body:
For Kedarkantha in December, January and February, a Decathlon down jacket rated around −10°C, such as the Forclaz MT500, is warm enough for most people, as long as you wear it over a thermal and a fleece. If you feel the cold easily, or you're going in the coldest weeks of January, the warmer MT900 (rated −18°C) gives you a comfortable margin. The lighter MT100 (rated −5°C) is enough in November, March and April, but on its own it's too thin for a mid-winter night at base camp.

The catch is that Decathlon's ratings are for when you're moving. Standing around at camp, the same jackets are rated much warmer. This guide explains what that means for Kedarkantha, how to layer, and whether to buy or rent. For the full kit list, see [What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list), and for our departures, the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Which Decathlon jacket ratings work for Kedarkantha in December and January?

Here's how the three Forclaz down jackets most trekkers look at compare, using Decathlon's own ratings.

- **Forclaz MT100 down:** active comfort rating about −5°C, static comfort rating about +5°C. Good for November, March, April; a mid layer in deep winter.
- **Forclaz MT500 down:** active comfort rating about −10°C, static comfort rating about 0°C. Good for December to February for most people, with good layers.
- **Forclaz MT900 down:** active comfort rating about −18°C, static comfort rating about −5°C. Good for coldest weeks of January; people who feel the cold.

**Note:** Ratings as published by Decathlon for each jacket worn over a base layer and a light fleece. "Active" means while walking; "static" means standing still.

What the numbers mean in practice. At Kedarkantha base camp in January, nights are often around −10°C to −15°C. While you walk, your body makes plenty of heat, so even a −5°C jacket can feel warm. The hard moments are the evening at camp, the queue for dinner and the summit start at 4 am, when you're standing in the cold. That's when the static rating matters, and why a −10°C jacket over two layers works better than a −5°C jacket alone.

More on how cold each campsite gets is in [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)

## Is layering better than one big jacket on Kedarkantha?

Yes. On Kedarkantha, a mid-range down jacket worn over good layers beats one very heavy jacket, for three reasons:

1. **You can adjust.** You'll walk in a T-shirt or thermal in the forest at midday, and need everything at 4 am. Layers let you add and remove warmth.
2. **You stay dry.** A huge jacket worn while climbing makes you sweat, and damp clothes are what make people cold at camp.
3. **It packs smaller.** A lighter jacket plus a fleece fits in your daypack for summit day.

A layering system that works in December and January:

- **Base layer:** Thermal top and bottom (synthetic or merino, not cotton). When: always at camp, often while walking.
- **Mid layer:** Fleece jacket. When: morning starts, evenings, summit day.
- **Insulation layer:** Down jacket, around −10°C rating. When: evenings, nights, summit start.
- **Shell layer:** Windproof or waterproof jacket. When: wind on the summit slopes, snowfall.
- **Extras:** Woollen cap, balaclava, liner and outer gloves. When: evenings and summit day.

The full method is in [How do you layer clothes for a Himalayan trek?](/blog/layering-for-trekking), and the fleece-versus-down question in [Fleece or down jacket: which do you need on a trek?](/blog/fleece-vs-down-jacket)

## What to look for when choosing a down jacket for Kedarkantha

- **A hood.** A down hood makes a big difference at night and on the summit.
- **The right size.** It should fit over your thermal and fleece without squeezing them. Compressed down is cold down.
- **Water resistance.** Down loses warmth when wet. Keep a shell or rain jacket over it during snowfall, and store it in a dry bag.
- **Women's and men's fits.** Decathlon makes both versions of most jackets; the fit matters more than the label.
- **Weight.** Lighter is nice, but warmth matters more on this trek.

If you're comparing beyond Decathlon, the ratings advice in [Which down jacket rating do you need for a winter trek?](/blog/down-jacket-for-winter-trek) applies to any brand.

## Down or padded jacket: which is better for Kedarkantha?

Decathlon sells two kinds of warm jacket: down, filled with feathers, and padded, filled with synthetic fibres.

- Down is warmer for its weight and packs small, which is why most winter trekkers choose it. Its weakness is water: wet down loses most of its warmth, so keep a shell over it in snowfall.
- Padded jackets are cheaper and keep more warmth when damp, but they're bulkier and heavier for the same warmth.

For Kedarkantha between December and February, a down jacket rated around −10°C is the usual choice. A padded jacket works well in November, March and April, or as a warm mid layer under a shell in deep winter. Decathlon also lists warmer padded models rated to around −10°C, which suit people on a tighter budget.

## Which jacket for which month on Kedarkantha?

As a simple guide, worn over a thermal and a fleece:

- **November and March:** an MT100 down or a good padded jacket is usually enough.
- **December to February:** an MT500 or warmer. If you feel the cold badly, consider the MT900 for January.
- **April and May:** a fleece with a light padded jacket for evenings and summit morning.
- **October:** as for November, since nights are cold even without snow.

Whatever you choose, test it at home on a cold evening with your layers underneath before the trek.

## Should you buy or rent a down jacket for Kedarkantha?

Buy if you'll trek in winter again, or you'll wear it in a cold city. A jacket you've worn before also fits better and you know how warm it is.

Rent if this is a one-off. Down jackets are among the most common items rented in Sankri and Dehradun. In peak weeks, good sizes go early, so rent the evening you arrive, check the zips and filling, and don't accept a jacket that's flat or smells damp ([Where can you rent trekking gear in Sankri?](/blog/rent-trekking-gear-sankri)).

Our wider view on what to buy and what to rent is in [Should you rent or buy trekking gear?](/blog/rent-or-buy-trekking-gear) and [Which Decathlon gear is worth buying for a Himalayan trek?](/blog/decathlon-gear-for-trek)

## Common mistakes when choosing a jacket for Kedarkantha

- **Relying on the jacket alone.** Without a thermal and fleece underneath, even a −10°C jacket feels cold at camp.
- **Walking uphill in the down jacket.** You'll sweat into it. Take it off while climbing, put it on when you stop.
- **Sleeping in it while damp.** If it got wet during the day, dry it or keep it outside your sleeping bag.
- **Ignoring hands and feet.** Most people feel cold first in their fingers and toes. Good gloves and woollen socks matter as much as the jacket ([Which gloves and socks keep you warm on a snow trek?](/blog/gloves-for-snow-trek)).

## Our short answer: which Decathlon jacket for Kedarkantha?

For most people in December to February: an MT500-level down jacket (around −10°C) over a thermal and a fleece, with a windproof shell, cap and two pairs of gloves. If you feel the cold or you're going in the coldest weeks of January, choose the MT900 or add a warmer mid layer. In November, March and April, an MT100 plus a fleece is enough.

Sleeping bags are provided on our treks, rated for winter nights, so your jacket only needs to keep you warm outside the tent. Dates and what's included are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Altitude Sickness: Risks and Signs
posts.excerpt: How likely altitude sickness is on Kedarkantha, where the risk rises, the early signs and what happens if you get it.
posts.body:
Yes, there's some risk of altitude sickness on Kedarkantha, but for most people it's low and mild. You sleep at up to about 11,250 ft and reach about 12,500 ft on the summit, which is high enough for headaches, poor sleep and breathlessness, especially on the night at base camp. Serious altitude illness is rare on this trek, because the climb is spread over three days. The key is to know the early signs, tell your mountain guide straight away, and descend if symptoms get worse.

Here's where the risk rises, what happens on summit day, how trekkers are checked, and what to do if you feel unwell. For the trek itself, see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

**Note:** This article is general information, not medical advice. If you have a health condition, talk to your doctor before a high-altitude trek.

## How high does the Kedarkantha trek go?

- **Sankri (6,455 ft / 1,967 m):** very low risk.
- **Juda ka Talab camp (8,860 ft / 2,700 m):** low risk; mild headaches are possible.
- **Base camp (11,250 ft / 3,430 m):** moderate risk; this is the night most people feel it.
- **Summit (12,500 ft / 3,810 m):** moderate risk, but you're only there briefly.

**Note:** Altitudes are commonly published figures.

Altitude sickness becomes more likely above about 8,000 ft (2,500 m), and the biggest factor is how high you sleep, and how fast you got there ([At what altitude does altitude sickness start?](/blog/altitude-sickness-height)).

## At which Kedarkantha campsites does the risk of altitude sickness rise?

Juda ka Talab, night 1 on the trail. You've climbed about 2,400 ft from Sankri. A mild headache or slightly restless sleep is common and usually settles overnight with water and rest.

Base camp, night 2 on the trail. This is the night most people notice the altitude. You've slept about 2,400 ft higher than the night before, and base camp is cold and exposed. Common feelings:

- A dull headache, especially in the evening
- Breathlessness when you walk uphill or bend over
- Poor sleep, waking up often
- Less appetite than usual

These are mild symptoms of acute mountain sickness, or AMS (the body's reaction to less oxygen in the air). On their own they're manageable, but they're the signs your mountain guide is watching for. Why sleep is harder up high is explained in [Why is it hard to sleep at high altitude?](/blog/sleep-at-high-altitude)

## What happens to altitude sickness risk on Kedarkantha summit day?

On summit morning you climb about 1,250 ft above base camp, then descend all the way to Juda ka Talab. Two things work in your favour:

1. **You don't sleep at the summit.** You're at the highest point for less than an hour.
2. **You descend the same day.** Going down is the fastest cure for altitude symptoms, and by the evening you're about 3,600 ft lower than the summit.

Breathlessness on the final steep section is normal for everyone. What isn't normal: a severe headache that doesn't ease, vomiting, confusion, stumbling or extreme tiredness. If you feel any of those before or during the climb, tell your mountain guide at once. They may decide you shouldn't go up, or should turn back. That's the right call ([How high is Kedarkantha peak, and how hard is summit day?](/blog/kedarkantha-height)).

## What are the early signs of altitude sickness on Kedarkantha?

- **Mild headache, eased by rest and water:** tell your mountain guide, drink water and rest. Don't climb higher that day if it gets worse.
- **Nausea or loss of appetite:** tell your mountain guide, and eat small, easy meals.
- Unusual tiredness, more than others in the group: tell your mountain guide and slow down.
- **Headache that gets worse despite rest:** don't go higher. Your mountain guide may decide you should go down.
- Vomiting, confusion, stumbling, or breathlessness at rest: this is an emergency. Go down immediately, with help.

The last item describes the serious forms, called HAPE (fluid in the lungs) and HACE (swelling of the brain). They're rare on Kedarkantha, but they're the reason the team carries oxygen and keeps an eye on everyone ([What is the difference between AMS, HAPE and HACE?](/blog/ams-hape-hace-difference)). The full list of symptoms is in [What are the early signs of altitude sickness on a trek?](/blog/altitude-sickness-symptoms)

## How does the Kedarkantha trek team check you each day?

On our Kedarkantha departures, the trek team carries an oximeter, a blood pressure monitor, oxygen and a full medical kit. In practice, checks usually look like this:

- **Morning and evening:** a quick oxygen and pulse reading with the oximeter, and a few questions: headache? sleep? appetite?
- **On the trail:** your mountain guide watches pace, breathing and mood. With a group of ten or fewer, it's easier to notice someone struggling early.
- **Before summit day:** a final check the evening before and again at the wake-up. Anyone with worsening symptoms stays at base camp or descends.

An oximeter reading is one useful clue, not a verdict. Low numbers are normal at altitude; how you feel matters as much as the number ([What does a pulse oximeter reading tell you on a trek?](/blog/oximeter-reading-at-altitude)).

Who decides? Your mountain guide. If they say you descend, you descend, with a member of the team. It's the rule that brings people home safely.

## How can you lower your risk of altitude sickness on Kedarkantha?

1. **Climb slowly.** Walk at a pace where you can still talk. The first hour out of Sankri is where people overdo it.
2. **Drink 3 to 4 litres a day.** Dehydration makes headaches worse and feels like AMS.
3. **Eat, even without appetite.** Your body needs fuel to cope with cold and altitude.
4. **No alcohol or sleeping pills.** Both affect breathing at night.
5. **Arrive healthy.** A cold or fever before the trek makes altitude harder ([Can you trek with a cold, cough or fever?](/blog/trek-with-cold-or-fever)).
6. **Speak up early.** Most problems are easy to manage when they're small.

What about Diamox? Some trekkers take acetazolamide (Diamox), a medicine that can help the body adjust to altitude. It isn't needed by most people on Kedarkantha, and it has side effects. Only take it on a doctor's advice ([Should you take Diamox before a trek?](/blog/diamox-for-trekking)).

More general advice is in [How do you prevent altitude sickness on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/how-to-prevent-altitude-sickness) and [What should you do if you get altitude sickness on a trek?](/blog/what-to-do-altitude-sickness)

## What should you do if you feel altitude sickness on Kedarkantha?

Most cases on this trek are mild and settle with rest. The key is to act early and honestly:

1. **Tell your mountain guide straight away.** Don't hide a headache because you're worried about missing the summit.
2. **Stop climbing for the day.** Rest at camp, drink water, and eat something light.
3. **Get checked.** The team measures your oxygen level and pulse and asks how you feel.
4. **Don't go higher until you feel better.** If symptoms ease overnight, you may continue the next day.
5. **Go down if it gets worse.** A worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, stumbling or breathlessness at rest means descending at once, with a member of the team. Going down even 1,000 to 1,500 ft often brings quick relief.
6. **Oxygen is first aid, not a cure.** It helps while you descend; it doesn't replace going down.

The nearest hospitals are several hours away by road from Sankri, which is why early action matters so much on this trek. More detail is in [What should you do if you get altitude sickness on a trek?](/blog/what-to-do-altitude-sickness)

## Does being fit protect you from altitude sickness on Kedarkantha?

No. Fitness makes the walking easier, but it doesn't change how your body reacts to thinner air. In fact, fit trekkers sometimes get symptoms because they walk too fast and climb too quickly in a day.

What matters more is how fast you gain height, how much you drink, whether you arrived healthy, and whether you've had altitude sickness before. That's why the Kedarkantha itinerary spreads the climb over three days, and why your mountain guide sets a slow pace even when you feel strong ([How fit do you need to be for a Himalayan trek?](/blog/how-fit-do-you-need-to-be-for-trekking)).

## Who should talk to a doctor before the Kedarkantha trek?

If you have a heart or lung condition, high blood pressure, severe anaemia, or you've had altitude sickness before, speak to your doctor before booking. They may still say yes, with precautions ([Can you trek with a medical condition?](/blog/trekking-with-medical-condition)).

For the whole trek, see [How hard is the Kedarkantha trek for a beginner?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-difficulty), or check dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: How safe is Kedarkantha when it is covered in snow?
posts.seo_title: Is Kedarkantha Safe in Snow? Risks and Precautions
posts.excerpt: How safe Kedarkantha is under snow, which sections need care, and the kit and checks that keep the risk low.
posts.body:
Kedarkantha is a safe trek in winter for most people, as long as you're properly prepared and walk with an experienced team. The snow itself isn't the danger. The real risks are slips on icy descents, cold injuries if you get wet, altitude symptoms at base camp, and bad weather on summit day. All four are well understood, and a good team manages them with the right kit, early starts, daily health checks and the willingness to turn back.

Here's which sections need care in snow, how cold it really gets, and the safety kit and checks that keep the risk low. For our departures, see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Which sections of the Kedarkantha trek need care in snow?

- **Sankri to Juda ka Talab:** a steep forest climb, with icy patches in the shade from late December. A slow pace, shoes with good grip and trekking poles help.
- **Juda ka Talab to base camp:** snow deepens above the treeline, and the trail can disappear after fresh snowfall. Follow your mountain guide's line and wear gaiters.
- **The final climb to the summit:** the steepest section, often hard snow or ice in the early morning. Microspikes, short steps and an early start help.
- **Summit back to base camp:** a steep descent on snow, on tired legs. Use poles and microspikes, and take slow, deliberate steps.
- **Base camp to Juda ka Talab:** a long descent where packed snow turns slippery. Keep a gap from the person ahead, and sit down on short steep bits if you need to.

**Note:** Sections and conditions vary with each winter.

Watch for hard ice. Between about December and mid-April, parts of the trail can freeze into a thin, clear layer of ice (often called verglas), especially in shaded forest early in the morning. It looks like a wet path, and it's far more slippery than snow. Put microspikes on before you reach it, not after the first slip.

The descent is where most slips happen. People relax after the summit, legs are tired, and packed snow on a downhill trail is slick. Most injuries on winter treks are sprained ankles, wrist injuries from falls and bruised knees, rather than anything dramatic ([How do you walk on snow without slipping?](/blog/walking-on-snow)).

What about avalanches? The standard Kedarkantha route follows ridges and open slopes that aren't known as avalanche paths in normal conditions. After very heavy fresh snowfall, though, steep slopes can be unstable, which is one reason a mountain guide may delay or cancel a summit attempt.

## How cold does Kedarkantha really get in winter?

Cold is the most constant challenge on a winter Kedarkantha trek.

- **Sankri:** nights around −4°C to 2°C in December and January, days in the sun 5°C to 12°C.
- **Juda ka Talab:** nights around −8°C to −4°C, days in the sun 2°C to 8°C.
- **Base camp:** nights around −15°C to −8°C, days in the sun 0°C to 7°C.

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

Cold itself is manageable. It becomes dangerous when it combines with wet. Sweat on the climb, melted snow in your socks, or a damp sleeping bag can quickly lead to hypothermia (the body losing heat faster than it makes it) or frostnip on fingers and toes. Staying dry is the single most important safety habit on this trek ([What is hypothermia and how do you spot it on a trek?](/blog/hypothermia-trekking), [What are chilblains and frostbite, and how do you prevent them?](/blog/chilblains-frostbite-trek)).

The full month-by-month picture is in [How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature)

## What safety kit and checks are in place on our Kedarkantha treks?

On our Kedarkantha departures, this travels with every group:

### Equipment

- Oxygen cylinder
- Oximeter and blood pressure monitor
- Full medical kit and a stretcher
- Microspikes and gaiters for every trekker when conditions need them
- Rope, helmet, ice axe and harness where conditions require them
- Walkie-talkies to keep the team in touch on the trail
- A satellite phone, available on request (there's no mobile signal on most of the trail)

### People

- A trek leader qualified in mountaineering and first aid
- Local mountain guides who know the slopes in every kind of snow
- Emergency porters available to help someone descend
- A maximum of ten trekkers, so nobody struggles unnoticed at the back of a big group

### Checks

- Oxygen and pulse readings each morning and evening
- A briefing the night before summit day, with a clear turnaround time
- A final check at the 3 am wake-up; anyone unwell stays back or descends

The general standard every team should meet is in [What safety equipment should a trek team carry?](/blog/trek-safety-equipment)

## Who decides when Kedarkantha is unsafe?

Your mountain guide. They may delay the summit start for weather, turn the group around partway, or skip the summit altogether if the snow is unstable, the wind is strong or visibility is poor. Their decision is final. It's the most important safety rule on any winter trek, and it's the reason most incidents never happen.

## What should you do to stay safe on Kedarkantha in snow?

1. Train for a month, so summit day doesn't leave you exhausted on the descent.
2. Wear trekking shoes with good grip, broken in before you arrive ([Which trekking shoes are good for a snow trek?](/blog/trekking-shoes-for-snow)).
3. Use microspikes when your guide says so, and practise putting them on at camp ([Do you need microspikes or crampons on a trek?](/blog/microspikes-for-trekking)).
4. Use trekking poles, especially on descents.
5. Keep a dry set of clothes for camp and sleeping only.
6. Wear sunglasses on snow to avoid snow blindness ([How do you avoid sunburn and snow blindness on a trek?](/blog/sunburn-snow-blindness-trek)).
7. Tell your guide early about headaches, numb toes or feeling unwell ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).
8. Stay with the group. Don't walk ahead out of sight in snow or fog.
9. Take insurance that covers trekking and evacuation ([Do you really need trekking insurance in India?](/blog/trekking-insurance-india)).

## What happens in an emergency on the Kedarkantha trek?

If someone is injured or seriously unwell, the team gives first aid and oxygen if needed, and helps them descend, with emergency porters and a stretcher if they can't walk. From Juda ka Talab, Sankri is a few hours down; from base camp, longer. A vehicle can take a patient from Sankri to a hospital, which is several hours away by road. Helicopter evacuation is rare and depends on weather and permissions ([What happens in a medical emergency on a remote trek?](/blog/emergency-on-trek)).

## How to walk safely on snow and ice on Kedarkantha

A few simple techniques prevent most slips. Your mountain guide will show you on the first snowy stretch, but it helps to know them before you go:

1. **Take short steps.** Short, flat-footed steps keep your weight over your feet, where it belongs.
2. **Kick steps going up.** On a steep snow slope, kick the toe of your shoe into the snow to make a small step, then stand on it.
3. **Lead with your heels going down.** On soft snow, press your heels in first, with your knees slightly bent.
4. **Use your poles.** Plant them before you move your feet, and shorten them for climbs and lengthen them for descents.
5. **Walk in the footsteps ahead.** The trail broken by the person in front is firmer than fresh snow beside it.
6. **Keep a gap.** A few metres from the person ahead gives you room if they slip.
7. **Put microspikes on early.** Fit them before the icy section, not after the first fall, and check the straps are tight.

Don't slide down slopes on your bottom unless your mountain guide says the slope is safe for it; hidden rocks and ice cause injuries ([How do you walk on snow without slipping?](/blog/walking-on-snow)).

## How to choose a safe operator for Kedarkantha in winter

Ask these questions before you book any winter departure, with us or anyone else:

- How big is the group, and how many mountain guides walk with it?
- What training do the mountain guides have, especially in first aid and winter conditions?
- Do you carry oxygen, a pulse oximeter, a stretcher and a full medical kit?
- Are microspikes and gaiters provided for everyone?
- What are the sleeping bags rated to?
- How does the team communicate on the trail, and with the office, when there's no signal?
- What is the plan if someone needs to be brought down, and who pays for it?
- Who decides to turn back on summit day, and has that happened before?

A good operator answers all of these clearly and without fuss ([What should you ask a trek operator before you book?](/blog/questions-to-ask-trek-operator)).

## Is Kedarkantha safe for beginners in winter?

Yes, for prepared beginners with a good team. Thousands of first-timers summit Kedarkantha each winter. The ones who have a hard time are usually untrained, poorly equipped or rushing. For how hard it is day by day, see [How hard is the Kedarkantha trek for a beginner?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-difficulty), and for the bigger safety picture, [Is trekking in the Himalayas dangerous?](/blog/is-himalayan-trekking-dangerous)

Dates and what's included on our departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: What do a typical breakfast, lunch and dinner look like on Kedarkantha?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Trek Food: Meals, Snacks and Water
posts.excerpt: What you eat on the Kedarkantha trek: breakfast, packed lunch, dinner, summit-day food and how dietary needs are handled.
posts.body:
On the Kedarkantha trek, you eat three freshly cooked meals a day plus snacks and hot drinks, prepared at camp by the trek cook. Food is vegetarian, with eggs. A typical day is a hot breakfast of poha, parathas or porridge with eggs, a simple hot lunch at camp or a packed lunch on the trail, soup and a snack in the evening, and dinner of dal, rice, roti and a vegetable, often with a dessert. Summit day is different: tea and a light snack before the 4 am start, energy food on the climb, and a proper meal once you're back down.

Here's what's served each day, when lunch is packed or hot, what summit-day food looks like, and how dietary needs work. On our departures, all meals from dinner on day 1 to dinner on day 5 are included; see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## What food is served each day on the Kedarkantha trek?

Menus vary with the cook, the season and what's available in Sankri, but a typical trek day looks like this:

- **Wake-up:** Tea or coffee brought to your tent
- **Breakfast:** Poha, upma, aloo paratha or porridge; boiled or scrambled eggs; bread with jam or peanut butter; tea, coffee, hot chocolate
- **Lunch:** Hot lunch at camp (rajma-chawal, khichdi, chole with rice) or a packed lunch on the trail (parathas, sandwiches, fruit, juice)
- **Evening:** Soup with a snack: pakoras, Maggi, popcorn or biscuits
- **Dinner:** Dal, rice, roti, one or two vegetable dishes, salad or pickle; a dessert like halwa, kheer or custard
- **Through the day:** Tea, hot water, and dry snacks from your own bag

The food is simple, filling and warm, built to give you energy in the cold. Most trekkers are surprised by how good it is, cooked on gas stoves in a kitchen tent at minus temperatures. For the wider picture of trek food, see [What food do you get on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/food-on-himalayan-trek)

## Kedarkantha trek meals, day by day

Day 1, Sankri. Dinner at the guesthouse after you arrive. Hot, home-style food, often with local touches like rajma or a seasonal vegetable.

Day 2, Sankri to Juda ka Talab. Breakfast at the guesthouse before you set off. The walk takes 4 to 5 hours, so lunch is usually either packed for the trail or served hot when you reach camp in the early afternoon. Evening soup and snacks, then dinner in the dining tent.

Day 3, Juda ka Talab to base camp. A shorter walk of 3 to 4 hours. Breakfast at camp, then lunch is usually hot at base camp. Dinner is early, because summit day starts in the middle of the night.

Day 4, summit day. See below.

Day 5, Juda ka Talab to Sankri. Breakfast at camp, a 3 to 4 hour walk down, and lunch in Sankri or on the way out.

## Is lunch packed or hot on the Kedarkantha trek?

Both, depending on the day.

- Hot lunch when you reach camp by early afternoon, which is most days on Kedarkantha because the walking days are short.
- Packed lunch when the walk is long or the group starts late, or on the descent. Expect parathas or sandwiches, a fruit, a juice box and a sweet.

Packed lunches are usually eaten at a sunny spot on the trail. In deep winter, cold food gets hard quickly, so keep your lunch near the top of your bag and eat it before it freezes.

## What do you eat on Kedarkantha summit day?

Summit day is the longest and coldest day, and the food is planned around a 4 am start.

- **About 3 am:** Tea or hot chocolate and biscuits or a light porridge, at your tent or in the dining tent
- **On the climb:** Your own snacks: dry fruit, chocolate, energy bars; a flask of hot water or tea if you carry one
- **On the summit:** A quick snack and a sip of something warm, weather permitting
- **Back at base camp, mid-morning:** A proper hot meal, often a brunch of parathas, eggs, poha or noodles
- **At Juda ka Talab, evening:** Soup, snacks and a full dinner; many groups have a small celebration

Eat even if you don't feel like it. At altitude, many people lose their appetite, especially at 3 am. Small, frequent bites keep your energy up for the climb and the long descent ([Why do you lose your appetite at altitude?](/blog/appetite-loss-altitude)).

## Which snacks should you carry on the Kedarkantha trek?

Meals are provided, but bring a small bag of your own snacks for the trail, roughly 150 to 200 g per day:

- Dry fruit and nuts (almonds, raisins, dates)
- Chocolate or energy bars
- Chikki or other jaggery sweets
- Electrolyte sachets for your water

Pack them where you can reach them without taking your bag off. There are small shops in Sankri for last-minute snacks. On the first day's climb, in busy months, villagers sometimes run a small stall selling tea and Maggi; carry a little cash in small notes if you'd like to stop, and bring your wrappers back down. Above Juda ka Talab, there's nothing to buy.

## Why does appetite drop on Kedarkantha, and how do you keep eating?

Many trekkers find they don't feel hungry above Juda ka Talab. Altitude often dulls appetite, and cold, tiredness and early starts don't help. At the same time, walking uphill in the cold uses far more energy than a normal day, so eating enough matters.

What helps:

- **Eat little and often.** A few bites every hour on the trail is easier than one big meal.
- **Start with soup.** Hot soup in the evening warms you, replaces salt and water, and wakes up your appetite.
- **Choose easy carbohydrates.** Rice, khichdi, porridge, noodles and potatoes are easier to eat at altitude than heavy, oily food.
- **Add a little sugar.** Sweet tea, chocolate and jaggery give quick energy on cold mornings.
- **Keep drinking.** Thirst also drops at altitude, and dehydration makes appetite worse.

If you can't eat at all, or feel sick at the sight of food, tell your mountain guide. Loss of appetite with a headache can be an early sign of altitude sickness ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).

## Where can you eat on the drive to Sankri?

The day-long drive from Dehradun to Sankri has a few regular food stops, usually small dhabas along the road around Mussoorie, Nowgaon, Purola and Mori. Expect simple, hot food: parathas, dal, rice, sabzi, Maggi and tea. Purola is known locally for its red rice, which some dhabas serve with rajma.

Meals on the road usually aren't part of the trek fee, so keep a few hundred rupees in cash for each travel day. Carry snacks and water for the drive too; on winding roads, lighter food is kinder to your stomach. In Sankri, guesthouses and small eateries serve hot meals in the evening.

## Can you get vegan, Jain or gluten-free food on Kedarkantha?

Usually, with notice. Tell the team when you book.

- **Vegan:** manageable; the main change is skipping ghee, butter, milk and paneer, and using plant milk or black tea.
- **Jain:** possible for most meals with advance notice, though the cook's options are more limited at camp.
- **Gluten-free:** rice, potatoes and dal make this workable, but bring some of your own gluten-free snacks.
- **Allergies:** tell us clearly when you book and again to the cook on day 1, especially for nut allergies.

More on special diets in [Can you get vegan, Jain or gluten-free food on a trek?](/blog/vegan-food-on-trek) If you'd like to try local dishes, Sankri's guesthouses sometimes serve Garhwali food like mandua roti or local red rice ([Which local Garhwali dishes should you try on a trek?](/blog/garhwali-food)).

## Where does drinking water come from on the Kedarkantha trek?

From taps in Sankri, and from mountain streams and springs on the trail. The team boils water for drinking, and hot water is available morning and evening to fill your bottles. In deep winter, when streams freeze, the team melts snow or carries water up ([Is stream water safe to drink on a trek?](/blog/drinking-water-on-trek)).

Carry two 1-litre bottles, and fill one with hot water at night to keep inside your sleeping bag. It keeps you warm and stops it freezing ([How do you stop water from freezing on a winter trek?](/blog/water-freezing-on-winter-trek)).

## Is alcohol or meat served on the Kedarkantha trek?

No. Food on our treks is vegetarian with eggs, and alcohol isn't allowed. Alcohol makes the cold and the altitude harder on your body.

For the rest of the trek day, see [What is a typical day like on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-itinerary), or check dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: What are the campsites on the Kedarkantha trek like?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Campsites: Juda ka Talab to Base Camp
posts.excerpt: Every campsite on the Kedarkantha trek: Sankri, Juda ka Talab and base camp, how cold each gets and what you see.
posts.body:
On the classic Kedarkantha route you stay in three places: a guesthouse in Sankri at about 6,455 ft, the forest campsite at Juda ka Talab at about 8,860 ft, and Kedarkantha base camp at about 11,250 ft, an open clearing above the treeline with the summit in view. Juda ka Talab is sheltered and the most social. Base camp is the coldest and the most beautiful. Most groups sleep at Juda ka Talab twice, on the way up and again after the summit.

Here's what each campsite is like, which is coldest, and what you see from each. Our departures use these camps; see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Which campsites are used on the Kedarkantha trek?

- **Night 1, Sankri (6,455 ft / 1,967 m):** Guesthouse.
- **Night 2, Juda ka Talab (8,860 ft / 2,700 m):** Tents in a forest clearing by a small lake.
- Night 3, Kedarkantha base camp (11,250 ft / 3,430 m): Tents on an open slope above the treeline.
- **Night 4, Juda ka Talab (8,860 ft / 2,700 m):** Same camp as night 2.
- **Night 5, Sankri, or onward travel (6,455 ft):** Guesthouse.

Altitudes are commonly published figures. Some operators use other camps, such as Hargaon on the descent. For the route variations, see [Which route is best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-route)

## Sankri: the guesthouse night before and after Kedarkantha

Sankri is the last village on the road and the start of the trek. You arrive after a long drive from Dehradun and stay in a simple guesthouse.

- **Rooms:** shared, usually triple, quad or five-sharing, with men and women in separate rooms on our treks.
- **Facilities:** beds with blankets, attached or shared bathrooms, hot water by bucket in most places, patchy electricity and phone signal.
- **What you do:** meet your mountain guide, check your gear, rent anything missing and get an early night.

More on the village is in [What is Sankri village like?](/blog/sankri-village) and on rooms in [Where should you stay in Sankri before a trek?](/blog/where-to-stay-in-sankri)

## Juda ka Talab: Kedarkantha's forest camp

After a 4 to 5 hour climb through pine and oak, you reach a clearing in the forest around a small lake. It's the first night in a tent for most trekkers.

- **Setting:** tall trees all around, the lake in the middle, and from late December, snow on the ground. In the coldest weeks the lake freezes over ([Is Juda ka Talab frozen in winter?](/blog/juda-ka-talab)).
- **Shelter:** the forest blocks most of the wind, so it often feels warmer than its height suggests.
- **Crowds:** it's the busiest camp on the trek, especially around Christmas and New Year, when many groups share the clearing ([Is overcrowding ruining popular treks like Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-crowded)).
- **Water:** from streams nearby, or snow melted by the team in deep winter.

You sleep here again on night 4, after the summit, tired and happy.

## Kedarkantha base camp: the high camp

A 3 to 4 hour climb from Juda ka Talab takes you through the last of the forest and out above the treeline. Base camp sits on an open slope, with the summit cone rising above it.

- **Setting:** wide snowfields, scattered trees below and big sky above. On a clear evening the peaks around you turn pink at sunset.
- **Exposure:** no forest shelter, so wind is common, especially in the late afternoon.
- **Cold:** the coldest night of the trek (see below).
- **Altitude:** the highest place you sleep. Mild headaches and poor sleep are common here ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).
- **Summit night:** you only sleep a few hours here before the 3 am wake-up.

## Which Kedarkantha campsite is coldest?

Base camp, by a clear margin.

- **Sankri:** nights around −4°C to 2°C in December and January, but you sleep indoors with blankets.
- **Juda ka Talab:** nights around −8°C to −4°C. Lower and sheltered by forest.
- **Base camp:** nights around −15°C to −8°C. The highest camp, open to the wind and pitched on snow.

**Note:** Typical ranges. Conditions vary from year to year.

In November, March and April, nights are much milder, but base camp is still usually below freezing. Inside the tent you'll be warm enough in a winter sleeping bag with dry thermals and a woollen cap. The tricky part is the hour after sunset and the summit start ([How cold does the Kedarkantha trek get?](/blog/kedarkantha-temperature), [How do you sleep warm in a tent in minus temperatures?](/blog/sleeping-warm-in-tent)).

## What views do you get from each Kedarkantha campsite?

- **Sankri:** forested hillsides and the first glimpse of snow peaks up the valley. Lovely in the evening light.
- **Juda ka Talab:** mostly a forest view, with the lake and trees. The beauty here is close-up: frost on branches, snow on the ice, quiet.
- **Base camp:** the best views of the trek before the summit. The Kedarkantha summit rises right above you, and on clear days you see snow peaks across the valley. Sunsets and starry skies here are some of the highlights of the whole trek.
- **Summit:** a wide view over the Garhwal Himalaya. Which peaks you can see is in [Which peaks can you see from the Kedarkantha summit?](/blog/kedarkantha-summit-view)

## What does a Kedarkantha campsite set-up include?

On our departures, each camp has:

- Sleeping tents: four-person all-season tents
- Sleeping bag, liner and mattress for every trekker
- A dining tent with camping stools, and a kitchen tent
- Two toilet tents with dry pits, dug and filled in by the team
- Safety kit: oxygen, oximeter, blood pressure monitor and a full medical kit

How tent sharing usually works on treks is in [How many people share a tent on a trek?](/blog/tent-sharing-trek), and what camping is like in general in [What is camping like on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/camping-on-trek)

## What about Hargaon and the other Kedarkantha campsites?

Some operators come down from the summit by a different trail and spend the last night at Hargaon, a clearing in pine and oak forest below base camp. It's quieter than Juda ka Talab and makes the trek a loop rather than an out-and-back.

On the less-used routes, groups camp at other clearings: Khujaai and Bhoja Dhadi on the Kotgaon side, and Julota and Pukhrola on the Gaichawan Gaon side, though names vary between operators. More on these in [Which route is best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-route)

Wherever you go, camping is only allowed at designated sites inside the sanctuary, and forest rules can change from season to season.

## Tips for a comfortable night at the Kedarkantha campsites

1. Organise your tent as soon as you arrive. Lay out your mattress and sleeping bag so the bag can loft (puff up) before night.
2. Keep your headtorch in the same pocket every night, so you can find it in the dark.
3. Leave the tent vents slightly open. It reduces the frost and condensation that forms inside on cold nights.
4. Keep your shoes in the tent porch, not outside, so they don't freeze or fill with snow.
5. Put your water bottle, phone and power bank inside your sleeping bag on very cold nights.
6. Visit the toilet tent before you settle in, and keep your shoes and a warm layer near the door in case you need to go out at night.

## How to keep the Kedarkantha campsites clean

These camps are used by thousands of trekkers every winter. Please:

1. Carry out every wrapper, wet wipe and battery.
2. Use only the toilet tents, never the lake edge or streams.
3. Don't build fires or cut branches.
4. Keep noise down after dark, for other groups and for the wildlife.

More in [What does Leave No Trace mean on a Himalayan trek?](/blog/leave-no-trace)

For how each day fits around the camps, see [What is a typical day like on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-itinerary), or check dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.seo_title: Mobile Network on Kedarkantha: Jio, BSNL, Airtel
posts.excerpt: Where your phone works on the Kedarkantha trek, which network to carry and how to stay in touch when there is no signal.
posts.body:
On the Kedarkantha trek, expect patchy mobile signal in Sankri and little or none on the trail. In Sankri, Jio and BSNL usually work, though not reliably. Above Sankri, signal mostly disappears, apart from brief bars at a few high, open points, sometimes including near the summit. Plan to be out of touch for three days, tell your family before you leave Sankri, and don't count on your phone in an emergency.

Here's where the last signal is, which network to carry, and how to send updates home. For everything else about the trek, see the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Which mobile networks work at each point on the Kedarkantha trek?

- **Dehradun to Purola:** Jio good, BSNL good, Airtel and Vi good. Normal signal on most of the road.
- **Purola to Sankri, via Mori:** Jio patchy, BSNL patchy, Airtel and Vi weak. Signal drops in and out on the drive.
- **Sankri:** Jio patchy, BSNL patchy, Airtel and Vi weak or none. Calls and messages usually work; data is slow and unreliable.
- **Sankri to Juda ka Talab:** Jio mostly none, BSNL mostly none, Airtel and Vi none. Occasional bars at open points.
- **Juda ka Talab:** Jio none, BSNL rare, Airtel and Vi none. Treat it as no signal.
- **Base camp:** Jio rare, BSNL rare, Airtel and Vi none. Brief signal at some spots on a clear day.
- **Summit:** Jio and BSNL possible but brief, Airtel and Vi none. Some trekkers report a few bars; don't rely on it.

**Note:** Network coverage changes as towers are added and as weather affects signal. These are based on recent trekker reports.

Which SIM to carry? If you can, carry two: Jio and BSNL are the most commonly reported to work around Sankri. Airtel and Vi are weaker here. A dual-SIM phone gives you the best chance.

## Where is the last mobile signal before the Kedarkantha trek?

For practical purposes, Sankri is your last reliable signal, and even there it comes and goes. Many trekkers find the signal gets weak soon after Purola, two to three hours before Sankri on the drive, so it's worth making important calls there. Before you start walking on day 2:

1. Call or message home with your plan and return date.
2. Send your family the operator's office number and, if you have it, your mountain guide's name.
3. Download offline maps and anything you want to read or listen to.
4. Switch off auto-updates and background data, so the phone doesn't drain hunting for signal.

You'll probably get signal again on the way back down to Sankri on day 5. More on Sankri's network and ATMs in [Is there an ATM and mobile network in Sankri?](/blog/sankri-atm-network)

## How do you send updates home from the Kedarkantha trek?

- **Agree a "no news is good news" plan.** Tell your family you'll be out of reach from day 2 to day 5, and when to expect your call.
- **Give them the office contact.** Your operator's office is the point of contact while you're out of signal. On our treks, the team stays in touch on the trail with walkie-talkies, and a satellite phone can be arranged on request, so urgent news can get through.
- **Use brief signal well.** If you get a few bars at base camp or on the summit, send a short text rather than trying a call or uploading photos.
- **Keep photos for later.** Uploads will fail on weak signal and drain your battery. Share them from Sankri or Dehradun.

## How do you keep your phone working in the cold on Kedarkantha?

Phones die fast in cold weather, especially when they keep searching for a signal.

1. Use airplane mode on the trail. It saves a lot of battery, and you can still use the camera.
2. Keep the phone warm. Carry it in an inside pocket by day and inside your sleeping bag at night.
3. Carry a power bank, 10,000 to 20,000 mAh, also kept warm. There's no electricity at the campsites ([How do you charge your phone on a trek?](/blog/charging-phone-on-trek)).
4. Lower the brightness and close unused apps.
5. Bring a spare cable, in case one breaks in the cold.

More tips are in [How do you keep phone batteries alive in the cold?](/blog/battery-drain-in-cold)

## What happens in an emergency on Kedarkantha without signal?

Because the trail has almost no signal, emergencies are handled by the team on the ground. On our departures:

- The mountain guide and trek team carry walkie-talkies to stay in touch on the trail.
- Oxygen, an oximeter and a full medical kit travel with every group.
- Emergency porters can help someone descend to Sankri, where there's road access and some signal.
- A satellite phone can be arranged on request for groups that want one.

This is one of the main reasons to trek with an experienced team rather than alone ([Is it safe to trek alone in winter near Kedarkantha?](/blog/kedarkantha-solo), [What happens in a medical emergency on a remote trek?](/blog/emergency-on-trek)).

## Can you use offline maps or a satellite device on Kedarkantha?

Offline maps work well. Your phone's GPS doesn't need mobile signal, so a map you download before Sankri will still show where you are on the trail. Download the area in your maps app, or a hiking app that uses OpenStreetMap, while you still have data. It's a useful backup, not a replacement for your mountain guide, especially when snow hides the path.

Satellite phones and personal satellite messengers are a different matter. In India they are tightly regulated, and using one generally needs permission from the government. Don't bring your own without checking first. On our treks, a satellite phone can be arranged on request for groups that want one.

## Should you buy a local SIM for the Kedarkantha trek?

If your current network is Airtel or Vi, a second SIM on Jio or BSNL gives you a better chance of signal around Sankri. A few things to know:

- Buy it in your home city or in Dehradun, not in Sankri. New SIMs need ID and can take a few hours to activate.
- Foreign nationals need their passport and visa to buy an Indian SIM, and the process takes longer.
- Recharge before you leave Dehradun. There's little chance to do it later.
- Use a dual-SIM phone so you don't have to swap cards on the trail.

## The upside of being offline on Kedarkantha

Many trekkers say three days without a phone was one of the best parts of the trek. No notifications, no emails, just the walk, the people around you and the mountains. It's worth leaning into.

For network on other treks, see [Is there mobile network on Himalayan treks?](/blog/mobile-network-on-trek) For the full overview of this trek, start with [What is the Kedarkantha trek like, and is it right for you?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-guide), or check dates on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

posts.title: Can you trek Kedarkantha solo, and is it safe alone in winter?
posts.seo_title: Kedarkantha Solo Trek: Is It Safe Alone in Winter?
posts.excerpt: Doing Kedarkantha as a solo traveller: joining a small group, rooms and tents, solo women, the risks of walking alone in snow, wildlife and costs.
posts.body:
Yes, you can do Kedarkantha as a solo traveller, and many people do. The usual way is to book a seat on a group departure: you travel to Sankri on your own, then walk with a small group, a mountain guide and a support team. You share a tent and a guesthouse room with other trekkers of the same gender, and you'll usually make friends by the end of day 2. What you shouldn't do is walk the trail completely alone in winter. Snow hides the path, fog can turn open slopes into a featureless white, there's no phone signal for most of the way, and the forest office generally won't issue a permit without a registered local guide.

Here's how solo trekking on Kedarkantha works, the real risks of walking alone in snow, how much wildlife matters, what it costs, and what solo women in particular want to know. Our open departures are on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).

## Is it allowed and safe to trek Kedarkantha solo?

Travelling solo: yes, and it's very common. On a typical winter departure, several trekkers in a group are on their own. Group treks are designed for this.

Walking alone without a guide: not really. Kedarkantha lies inside the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary and National Park, and recent reports say the forest office at Sankri issues permits only to trekkers with a registered local guide. More on the rules in [Do you need a permit for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-permit) and [Can you do the Kedarkantha trek without a guide or agency?](/blog/kedarkantha-without-guide)

So your realistic choices as a solo trekker are:

- **Join a group departure:** you book one seat and everything is arranged. Best for most solo trekkers, especially first-timers.
- **Hire a private local guide:** just you and a guide, plus a cook or porter. Best for experienced trekkers who want their own pace.
- **Go with friends, independently:** you organise the guide, gear and food yourselves. Best for groups of three or more with winter experience.

## What are the risks of walking the Kedarkantha trail alone in winter?

Even if the rules allowed it, walking Kedarkantha alone in snow is a bad idea. These are the reasons mountain guides give most often:

1. **Losing the trail.** Fresh snow covers the path, often overnight. Above Juda ka Talab the forest opens out into wide slopes, and in fog or falling snow they look the same in every direction. On your own, a wrong turn can take you away from the trail without you noticing until it's late ([What should you do if you get lost on a trek?](/blog/lost-on-trek)).
2. **An injury with no one to help.** A twisted ankle on icy ground is a minor problem in a group and a serious one alone. You can't carry your pack, keep warm and get yourself down a snowy slope at the same time.
3. **Cold that creeps up on you.** Hypothermia (when your body loses heat faster than it makes it) makes people tired, clumsy and confused, which is exactly when they stop noticing it. A companion spots the signs; you might not ([What is hypothermia and how do you spot it on a trek?](/blog/hypothermia-trekking)).
4. **Altitude symptoms you can't judge.** A headache at base camp is common. Deciding whether it's mild or getting worse is harder when you're alone, cold and tired ([Is there a risk of altitude sickness on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-altitude-sickness)).
5. **No way to call for help.** Signal is patchy in Sankri and mostly gone above it ([Is there mobile network on the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-network)). On weekdays outside peak weeks, you may not meet another group for hours.
6. **Weather decisions with no second opinion.** Knowing when to turn back is the most important safety skill on a winter summit. Alone, it's easy to push on because you've come so far.

## Is wildlife a danger for solo trekkers on Kedarkantha?

Much less than people fear. The Govind Wildlife Sanctuary is home to Himalayan black bears, leopards and smaller animals like foxes, deer and martens, as well as birds such as the Himalayan monal ([Which animals live in the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary?](/blog/govind-wildlife-sanctuary-animals)).

In winter:

- Black bears are mostly inactive, sleeping through the coldest months in many cases.
- Leopards live in the area but avoid people, and attacks on trekkers are extremely rare.
- Smaller animals, like foxes, are sometimes seen around campsites looking for food scraps.
- Dogs from the villages often follow groups up the trail. They're usually friendly.

Sensible habits keep the risk tiny: don't leave food or waste outside your tent, don't wander away from camp alone at dawn or dusk, and never feed wildlife or village dogs. If you see a large animal, stay calm, don't run, make yourself look big and back away slowly ([What should you do if you see a bear or leopard on a trek?](/blog/wildlife-on-trek)). The real dangers for a solo walker are getting lost, getting hurt and getting cold.

## How do you join a Kedarkantha group as a solo trekker?

1. **Pick your dates.** Choose a departure that fits your leave. Weekday starts and months like February are quieter ([Which months are best for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/best-time-for-kedarkantha-trek)).
2. **Book a single seat.** You pay the same per-person fee as everyone else. There's usually no "solo supplement" for a shared tent.
3. **Read about your mountain guide.** On our departures, every group has a named mountain guide whose certificates and reviews you can see before you pay.
4. **Plan your journey to Sankri.** Overnight train or bus to Dehradun, then a 9 to 10 hour drive. Our Dehradun transport add-on means you travel with the rest of the group from Dehradun ([How do you get from Dehradun to Sankri by bus, jeep or taxi?](/blog/dehradun-to-sankri)).
5. **Meet the group in Sankri.** Your mountain guide meets everyone on the evening of day 1. By the next evening, after a day of walking and a meal in the dining tent, most solo trekkers feel part of the group.

More general advice is in [Can you join a group trek on your own?](/blog/join-group-trek-alone)

## Where do you sleep as a solo trekker on Kedarkantha?

- **In Sankri:** shared guesthouse rooms, triple to five-sharing, with men and women in separate rooms on our treks.
- **On the trail:** shared tents with other trekkers of the same gender. If you'd prefer a single tent, ask when you book; it may be possible for an extra charge.
- Couples and friends who book together can usually share a tent.

How tent sharing works on most treks is in [How many people share a tent on a trek?](/blog/tent-sharing-trek)

## Why being in a group matters most on Kedarkantha in winter

Winter on Kedarkantha means snow, cold and short days, and that's when being part of a group matters most.

- **Navigation:** snow hides the trail, and your mountain guide sets the route.
- **Safety:** someone notices if you're cold, unwell or slipping behind.
- **Shared warmth:** a dining tent full of people is warmer than a tent on your own.
- **Summit day:** you start at 3:30 to 4 am in the dark. Walking in a line behind a mountain guide is far safer than finding your own way ([How high is Kedarkantha peak, and how hard is summit day?](/blog/kedarkantha-height)).

On our departures, groups are capped at ten trekkers, with a named mountain guide. A small group feels personal, and the guide can walk at the pace of the slowest person.

## Is Kedarkantha safe for a solo woman?

Yes. Solo women are a large share of trekkers on Kedarkantha, and many first-time women trekkers choose it because it's well supported. What helps:

- **Separate rooms and tents.** On our treks, guesthouse rooms are separated by gender, and you'll share a tent with other women.
- **A named mountain guide.** You know exactly who you'll be walking with before you book.
- **Small groups.** A group of up to ten feels personal; everyone knows everyone.
- **Private toilet tents.** Two toilet tents at each camp.
- **Speaking up.** If anything makes you uncomfortable, tell your mountain guide. Requests about tent arrangements are normal and welcome.

More detail is in [Is it safe for a solo woman to trek in Uttarakhand?](/blog/solo-female-trek-uttarakhand), and practical tips in [What tips help women on their first Himalayan trek?](/blog/tips-for-women-trekkers)

## What does the Kedarkantha trek cost for a solo trekker?

On a group departure, you pay the same per-person fee as everyone else. Our Kedarkantha fee is ₹10,450 plus 5% GST, Sankri to Sankri, with an optional Dehradun transport add-on at ₹2,200 plus GST. The full trip, including travel from Delhi, usually adds up to roughly ₹16,000 to ₹22,000 ([How much does the Kedarkantha trek cost in total?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-cost)).

Hiring a private guide as a solo traveller costs more per person, because you pay for the guide, cook and porters on your own.

## Safety tips for solo trekkers on Kedarkantha

1. Don't walk the trail alone. Join a small group, or hire a registered local guide in Sankri ([How do you hire a local guide in Sankri safely?](/blog/local-guide-sankri)).
2. Tell someone your plan. Share your dates, route and your operator's contact with family before you lose signal in Sankri.
3. Arrive in Sankri on time, ideally by the evening of day 1, so you meet the group before the walk.
4. Carry the basics in your daypack: headtorch with spare batteries, warm layer, water, snacks, a small first aid kit, a whistle and a power bank.
5. Stay with your group on the trail, especially in snow or fog. Don't walk ahead out of sight.
6. Know your turnaround time on summit day, and stick to it.
7. Keep a dry set of clothes for camp. Wet clothes are what make cold dangerous.
8. Take insurance that covers trekking and evacuation ([Do you really need trekking insurance in India?](/blog/trekking-insurance-india)).
9. Pack light and well. No one else will carry your extras ([What do you need to pack for the Kedarkantha trek?](/blog/kedarkantha-trek-packing-list)).

10. Say yes to the evening chai. It's where the group becomes friends.

When you're ready, pick a date and book a seat on the [Kedarkantha trek page](/treks/kedarkantha).
